name: Mangup (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Principality of Theodoro; en.wikipedia Siege of Mangup (after Pilat & Cristea 2017); A. A. Vasiliev, The Goths in the Crimea (1936)
borderline: Theodoro was a Greek-speaking Orthodox principality with a mixed (Greek, Gothic, Alan, Circassian) population and a dynasty of disputed origin; flagged as borderline by the brief.
note: The siege followed the fall of Caffa (6 June 1475); en.wikipedia dates it September–December, other accounts start it in the summer. About 300 Moldavian ('Wallachian') troops sent by Stephen the Great helped hold it. After five assaults and famine Mangup surrendered at the end of December 1475; Alexander was executed in Constantinople.

name: Oitylo passes
place: Passes near Oitylo (between Passavas and Oitylo), Mani
sources: Sathas, Τουρκοκρατούμενη Ελλάς; en.wikipedia Krokodeilos Kladas; himara.gr, 'Ο εκ Χειμάρρας οπλαρχηγός Κροκόδειλος Κλαδάς' (after Sathas, Miller and Venetian records)
borderline: No standard battle name; known from Sathas and Venetian reports. Kladas' force mixed Maniots with his stradioti.
note: Ottoman losses reportedly c. 700; the survivors fell back on Mystras/Sparta (19 January 1481 in Sathas' account). en.wikipedia places the rebel victory in February 1481 'between Passavas and Oitylo'.

name: Himara (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Albanian Rebellion of 1481–1484; en.wikipedia Himara; himara.gr article on Kladas (Italian source quoted)
borderline: Part of Gjon Kastrioti II's Albanian rebellion; the Himara rebels are claimed by both Greek and Albanian historiography. Kladas came with Neapolitan galleys.
note: The rising spread to some 50 villages; a 3,000-strong Ottoman relief force under Süleyman Pasha was routed (c. 1,000 killed or captured) and the castle fell on 31 August 1481; Sopot was taken later. The Ottomans retook Himara in summer 1484.

name: Ioannina (1611)
sources: en.wikipedia Dionysios Skylosophos; Τα Νέα 17.8.2000 'Διονύσιος ο Φιλόσοφος' (after Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους, vol. Ι); Vakalopoulos, Ιστορία του Νέου Ελληνισμού, vol. 3
note: About 700–1,100 poorly armed peasants from Thesprotia entered the town at night and burned the governor's residence; at dawn Osman Pasha's mounted guard dispersed them and c. 200 who hid in the lake reeds were burned. Dionysios was caught days later and flayed alive. His earlier Thessaly rising (November 1600) produced no named battle.

name: Koroni (siege, 1685)
sources: en.wikipedia Morean War; en.wikipedia Battle of Kalamata (1685); Setton, Venice, Austria, and the Turks
borderline: Venetian siege; the Maniot contingent was small (c. 230 men under Pavlos Makris).
note: An Ottoman relief army was beaten off in early August; the fortress was stormed on 11 August and the garrison massacred. Its fall set off the Maniot rising against the castles of Mani.

name: Zarnata (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Morean War; en.wikipedia Battle of Kalamata (1685)
borderline: Ended in a negotiated surrender; the scale of fighting is unclear.
note: Besieged by the Maniots after Koroni fell; surrendered to the Venetians and Maniots on 10 September 1685, the garrison being allowed to leave for Kalamata.

name: Kalamata (1685)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kalamata (1685); en.wikipedia Morean War; Setton, Venice, Austria, and the Turks
note: c. 11,500 Venetians and Saxons with Maniots against c. 6,000 infantry and 2,000 sipahis; the Maniots held the heights on the Venetian right and pursued the Ottomans through the town. Kalamata's castle was then razed.

name: Kelefa (siege, 1685)
place: Kelefa castle, above Oitylo bay, Mani
sources: en.wikipedia Morean War; en.wikipedia Battle of Kalamata (1685)
borderline: Ended in a capitulation once Venetian forces arrived.
note: The Maniots besieged the Ottoman garrison after Koroni fell; divided by feuds, they needed Venetian ships and troops, and the garrison capitulated in late September 1685. Venice then garrisoned Kelefa.

name: Koroni (siege, 1770)
sources: en.wikipedia Orlov revolt; el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά; en.wikipedia Siege of Coron (1770)
borderline: Russian-led siege; the Greek (Western) Legion fought as a distinct allied unit.
note: The fortress held out for about six weeks and the siege was given up when the Russians turned on Navarino. en.wikipedia's separate 'Siege of Coron (1770)' article claims the town was taken and then retaken in June; the standard account (Orlov revolt article, Vakalopoulos) is a failed siege.

name: Tripolitsa (1770)
sources: el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά; en.wikipedia Orlov revolt
note: The rebels besieging Tripolitsa were routed by Turco-Albanian reinforcements, and a massacre of the town's Greek inhabitants followed. The date is el.wikipedia's (calendar style not stated).

name: Mystras (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Orlov revolt; el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά
note: The Eastern Legion (mostly Maniots) took Mystras after a short siege and many of its Muslim inhabitants were killed; a provisional government under Antonios Psaros was set up there. Turco-Albanian forces later left the town in ruins.

name: Navarino (siege, 1770)
sources: en.wikipedia Orlov revolt; el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά
borderline: Russian-led siege; the Greek role was secondary.
note: The fortress surrendered after a short siege and became the Russian base; it was abandoned after the failure at Methoni (el.wikipedia's dates for this are inconsistent).

name: Methoni (siege, 1770)
sources: el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά; en.wikipedia Siege of Coron (1770)
borderline: Russian-led siege; Greek irregulars as an allied unit.
note: The besiegers were routed by an Ottoman relief army; el.wikipedia calls this defeat the decisive end of the Orlov enterprise in the Peloponnese. The Russians then left Navarino for the Aegean.

name: Krapi (1770)
place: Krapi plateau, between Apokoronas and Sfakia, Crete
sources: en.wikipedia Daskalogiannis; Detorakis, History of Crete
note: The rising began on 25 March 1770 and at first drove the Turks back; after the Ottomans massed at Vrysses (May), the rebels were crushingly defeated on the Krapi plateau and took to the mountains. Daskalogiannis surrendered in 1771 and was flayed alive in Heraklion on 17 June 1771.

name: Vromopigada
place: Vromopigada plain, between Skoutari and Parasyros, East Mani
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Vromopigada; en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1770); Daskalakis, Η Μάνη και η Οθωμανική Αυτοκρατορία (1923); Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos, Deep into Mani
note: Preceded by the three-day defence of the Grigorakis tower at Skoutari (c. 15 men), which the Ottomans mined and blew up. A Maniot night attack routed the camp; the dead were thrown into wells, hence the name ('dirty wells'). en.wikipedia names the Ottoman commander both Hadji Osman and Hasan Ghazi.

name: Trikorfa (1779)
war: Expulsion of the Albanians from the Morea (1779)
place: Trikorfa passes, north-west of Tripolitsa, Arcadia
sources: el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά (after Theodoros Kolokotronis, Διήγησις συμβάντων)
borderline: Known from Kolokotronis' memoirs; the opponents were Albanian irregulars in revolt against the Porte, who were being destroyed by Hasan Pasha's army (so the klephts fought alongside the Ottoman effort).
note: With c. 1,000 men Kolokotronis held the passes against Albanian bodies of 4,000 and 6,000 fleeing Hasan Pasha's victory at Tripolitsa (10 July 1779) and blocked their retreat.

name: Kastanitsa (1780)
war: Hasan Pasha's pacification of the Morea (1779–80)
place: Kastanitsa (Kastania), towers of Panagiotaros Venetsanakis, Mani
sources: el.wikipedia Ορλωφικά; Theodoros Kolokotronis, Διήγησις συμβάντων της ελληνικής φυλής; en.wikipedia Theodoros Kolokotronis
note: Klephts and Maniots held two towers for twelve days; most defenders, including Theodoros Kolokotronis' father, were killed, and the ten-year-old Theodoros was among the few survivors. el.wikipedia does not name the place; Kolokotronis' memoirs give Kastanitsa (placed in Mani, though some identify it with Kastanitsa in Kynouria).

name: Kastellorizo (1788)
sources: en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis; en.wikipedia Ottoman Greece; samos-web.aegean.gr Megisti ('Katsonis will free the island in July 1788'); neoskosmos.com (Malkidis): 'πολιόρκησε και γκρέμισε το οχυρό το 1788'; en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis ('destruction of a Turkish pirate base at Kastellorizo')
borderline: Capture of a fort used as a pirate base; the extent of resistance is unclear.
note: Katsonis' flotilla (sailing under a Russian commission) besieged the Ottoman fort, used as a pirate base, took it and demolished it; the Ottomans reoccupied the island in 1797.

name: Karpathos (1788)
sources: el.wikipedia Λάμπρος Κατσώνης; en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis; Peppa, speech on Lambros Katsonis (Dimos Levadeon)
note: Katsonis fought off the pursuing Ottoman fleet; the victory won him promotion and Catherine II's order that his squadron be styled a fleet of the Russian Empire.

date: June / 4 July 1789 (Peppa: 4 July; en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790): June 1789)
name: Syros–Mykonos (1789)
place: Waters between Syros, Tinos and Mykonos
sources: Peppa, speech on Lambros Katsonis (Dimos Levadeon); en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790) (background); en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis; dimoslevadeon.gr Peppa speech ('Στις 4 Ιουλίου ο Κατσώνης συναντήθηκε με σημαντική τουρκική δύναμη μεταξύ Σύρου και Μυκόνου και τη διασκόρπισε'); en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790): 'in June he defeated a Turkish fleet of 14 vessels between Syros and Mykonos' (summer 1789)
borderline: No standard battle name; the exact day differs between sources (June or 4 July 1789, possibly an Old/New Style difference).
note: Katsonis, newly based on Kea, met and dispersed an Ottoman squadron of 14 vessels between Syros and Mykonos. The 1788 dating in en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis (3 June 1788, Tinos–Mykonos) conflicts with en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790) and Greek sources, which put it in 1789. A second victory, between Syros and Delos, followed in July 1789.

date: 3–4 August 1789 (Peppa: 3 August; en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790): 4 August)
name: Makronisos (1789)
winner_first: Greek privateers beat Barbary corsairs & Ottomans
sources: Peppa, speech on Lambros Katsonis (Dimos Levadeon); en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790) (background); en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis; dimoslevadeon.gr Peppa speech ('Στις 3 Αυγούστου συνάντησε τουρκοαλγερινό στολίσκο στο στενό της Μακρονήσου ... τον ανάγκασε να καταφύγει στο Ναύπλιο'); en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790): 'defeating a joint Turkish and Algerian fleet off Eleni (Makronisos)', 4 August [1789]
borderline: No standard battle name (en.wikipedia Battle of Andros (1790) calls the site 'Eleni (Makronisos)').
note: Eight 32-gun Algerian xebecs (a Turco-Algerian squadron) were beaten, two sunk, and the rest chased into Nafplio. Days later an Ottoman fleet of 26 ships nearly trapped Katsonis at Kea and burned its harbour.

name: Andros (1790)
place: Off Cape Kafireas (Cavo Doro), between Euboea and Andros
winner_first: Ottomans & Barbary corsairs beat Greek privateers
sources: en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis; el.wikipedia Λάμπρος Κατσώνης; Peppa, speech on Lambros Katsonis; Hellenic Maritime Museum, painting no. 9463
note: On the first day Katsonis' nine ships beat off 16 Ottoman ships; next morning 13 Algerian ships joined them and his flotilla was overwhelmed. He burned his flagship Athena of the North (Minerva del Nord) and escaped with two ships to Kythira; Greek accounts give c. 565–650 of his men killed and 53 captured. The Hellenic Maritime Museum dates the battle 6 April 1790.

date: June 1792 (probably 28 June; also given as 8 June), three days
name: Porto Kagio (1792)
sources: en.wikipedia Lambros Katsonis; el.wikipedia Λάμπρος Κατσώνης; Peppa, speech on Lambros Katsonis
note: Katsonis had refused the 1791–92 peace and fortified Porto Kagio; about 30 Ottoman warships led by a French frigate (two French ships in el.wikipedia) attacked, and the fight went on for three days at sea and ashore. His ships were lost and he escaped to Kythira and Ithaca; Androutsos' men then fought their way overland (Androutsos' march, no single named battle).

name: Souli (1792)
place: Kiafa and the Souli villages, Thesprotia
sources: en.wikipedia Souliote War (1789–1793); en.wikipedia Souliotes; Perraivos, Ιστορία του Σουλίου και της Πάργας
note: Ali's army (c. 8,000–10,000) took Kiafa village but c. 1,300 Souliotes counter-attacked from the heights and routed it. Perraivos gives 2,000 Muslim Albanian and 74 Souliote dead (97 wounded); a Venetian chronicle gives 600 Ottoman dead. Greek accounts date the battle differently (around 20 July).

name: Nicopolis (1798)
winner_first: Ali Pasha beat French & Greek rebels
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nicopolis (1798); en.wikipedia Ali Pasha of Yanina
note: Ali (4,000–11,000 men) overwhelmed 300–600 French troops and their Greek auxiliaries; the Prevezan guard held the right centre until about noon. Ali's men then sacked Preveza and executed hundreds of its inhabitants.

name: Souli (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Souliotes; en.wikipedia Souliote War (1803); en.wikipedia Fotos Tzavelas; Perraivos, Ιστορία του Σουλίου και της Πάργας
note: Ali's assault of June–July 1800 (c. 11,500 men) failed and he ringed Souli with towers. The final campaign took Kakosouli by treachery (3 September 1803); after the last fight at Kiafa and Kougi (7 December) the Souliotes capitulated on 12 December and left for Parga. The later attacks on departing Souliotes (Zalongo and others) are treated as massacres.

name: Kougi
sources: en.wikipedia Souliote War (1803); en.wikipedia Souliotes; Perraivos, Ιστορία του Σουλίου και της Πάργας
borderline: A last stand inside the siege of Souli that ended with the monk Samuel blowing up the powder magazine; often treated as an event rather than a battle.
note: The last battle of Souli was fought at Kiafa and Kougi on 7 December 1803; after the capitulation (12 December) Samuel and a few men stayed in Kougi and blew up the magazine as Ali's troops entered. Exact date of the explosion varies (13–14 December).

name: Marathonisi (siege, 1803)
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1803); en.wikipedia Mani Peninsula; Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos, Deep into Mani; en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1803) (after Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos); en.wikipedia Tzanetos Grigorakis (1803: Kranae castle could not be demolished 'despite the 2,000 cannonballs'; Antonbey then made bey and Tzanetos fled to Zakynthos)
borderline: Thinly sourced; a blockade and bombardment more than a battle.
note: The Kapudan Pasha's Turco-Albanian force camped at Gytheio and blockaded and bombarded Grigorakis' island fort; Grigorakis slipped out at night and fled inland, and the Ottomans withdrew to Tripolitsa without subduing Mani.

name: Seltsou (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Souliotes; Perraivos, Ιστορία του Σουλίου και της Πάργας
note: About 1,200 Souliotes of the Botsaris clan who had left Souli were besieged in Agrafa; in the final assault on 7 April 1804 most were killed (tradition has women throwing themselves into the Acheloos) and c. 80 escaped. en.wikipedia calls it the Agrafa siege without naming the monastery.

name: Lefkada (siege, 1807)
place: Lefkada channel (Santa Maura fortress and Teke), Lefkada
winner_first: Septinsular Rep. & Russians beat Ali Pasha
sources: en.wikipedia Ali Pasha of Yanina; Woodhouse, Capodistria
borderline: A stand-off with skirmishes and bombardment across the channel rather than a pitched battle.
note: Kapodistrias organised Greek volunteers, c. 3,000 irregular riflemen (klephts and armatoles from the mainland) and the Russian troops; Ali gave up and left with 1,600 men to meet the Sultan's envoys.

name: Marathonisi (siege, 1807)
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1807); en.wikipedia Mani Peninsula; Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos, Deep into Mani; en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1807), whose only source is Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos, Deep into Mani; no Greek source found (the ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ Mani booklet and other Greek pages checked are silent)
borderline: Thinly sourced; a blockade and bombardment more than a battle.
note: A larger Turco-Albanian force ravaged the country round Gytheio and besieged Antonobey in his island fort by sea and land; he held out until the Ottomans gave up the siege.

name: Skoutari (1815)
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1815); en.wikipedia Mani Peninsula; Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos, Deep into Mani; en.wikipedia Ottoman invasion of Mani (1815) (cites Showalter, Revolutionary Wars 1775–c.1815, Encyclopedia of Warfare, and Greenhalgh & Eliopoulos): Kapudan Pasha's landing at Skoutari repulsed by Theodoros Grigorakis, 115 Ottoman and 30 Maniot dead
borderline: Known only from popular secondary works; historicity and details doubtful.
note: The Skoutariots attacked an Ottoman landing party on the beach and drove it back to the ships (115 Ottoman and 30 Maniot dead); described as the last Ottoman invasion of Mani.

name: Variades (1820)
sources: en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris; en.wikipedia Souliotes
note: After the Souliotes changed sides to Ali (coalition of 4 December 1820), Botsaris seized the fort of Variades from the Sultan's forces besieging Ioannina and fortified himself there.

name: Kompsades
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Κομψάδων (title and date); en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris
note: el.wikipedia dates it 22 December 1820; a Souliote victory.

name: Kalavryta (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία και απελευθέρωση των Καλαβρύτων (title and dates); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως, vol. 1; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 1
note: The Muslim garrison shut itself in the towers of Kalavryta and surrendered on 21 March (O.S.). Traditional accounts date the start of the siege to 21 March and the surrender to 26 March; dates here follow el.wikipedia.

name: Patras (1821)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Patras (1821); el.wikipedia Ξεσηκωμός της Πάτρας (title and date); Trikoupis vol. 1; Finlay vol. 1
note: The Greeks took the town and besieged the Ottomans in the citadel. On 3 April Yusuf Pasha landed from Rio, relieved the citadel and burned the town, and the besiegers scattered. en.wikipedia labels it a 'Greek victory', meaning the rising itself. Fighting began on 21–22 March; the start date follows el.wikipedia. The later siege of Patras (1822) is a separate entry for the next batch.

name: Malandrino
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Μαλανδρίνου (title and dates only)
note: el.wikipedia (24–27 March 1821): the Turks were taken prisoner.

name: Navarino (siege, 1821)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία του Νεοκάστρου (title and dates); en.wikipedia Siege of Navarino (disambiguation) and Navarino massacre; Finlay vol. 1
note: The starving garrison capitulated in early August and most of the Muslim population was then massacred (Navarino massacre, not a separate entry). Not to be confused with the naval battle of Navarino (1827), fought by the Allied fleets alone.

name: Agios Athanasios (Karytaina)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αγίου Αθανασίου Καρύταινας (title and date); Kolokotronis, Διήγησις συμβάντων της ελληνικής φυλής
borderline: Outcome based on Kolokotronis's memoirs; the el.wikipedia article could not be read to confirm it.
note: The Greeks besieging the Muslims in Karytaina castle fled at the approach of a relief force from Tripolitsa, leaving Kolokotronis with a handful of men at the chapel of Agios Athanasios. The besieged Muslims were then withdrawn to Tripolitsa.

name: Chlemoutsi (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία του Χλεμουτσίου (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: neutral outcome (ουδέτερη έκβαση).

name: Monemvasia (siege, 1821)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Monemvasia (1821); el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Μονεμβασίας (title and dates); Fotakos (Chrysanthopoulos), Απομνημονεύματα
note: en.wikipedia and el.wikipedia give a start of 15 March. Chrysanthopoulos (Fotakos) puts it after 25 March, as here. The fighting included bombardment and a failed sortie of about 150 men. The garrison surrendered on 23 July and was shipped to Asia Minor.

name: Salona (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία των Σαλώνων (title and dates); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: The garrison shut in the castle surrendered on 10 April.

name: Lidoriki (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία του Λιδωρικίου (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: after two days the besieged Turks surrendered.

name: Livadeia (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Λιβαδειάς (title and dates); en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; Trikoupis vol. 1
note: The Greeks took the town on 31 March. The garrison held out in the castle tower until 4 April. Omer Vrioni retook Livadeia on 10 June 1821.

name: Atalanti (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Αταλάντης (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: Diakos sent Antonios Kontosopoulos to free Atalanti (27 March 1821).

name: Nafplio (siege, 1821–1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία του Ναυπλίου (title and dates); Trikoupis vols. 1–2; Finlay vol. 1
note: A land and sea blockade (Spetsiot ships under Bouboulina) with sorties. A night escalade under Demetrios Ypsilantis failed in December 1821. Staikopoulos's night capture of Palamidi on 30 November 1822 is a distinctly named action for the 1822 batch. el.wikipedia ends the siege on 4 December 1822.

name: Vlachokerasia
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Βλαχοκερασιάς (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia (10 April 1821): a Greek camp was attacked by 3,000 Turks and broken up; Nikolopoulos and Venetsianakos fell.

name: Mendenitsa (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Μενδενίτσας (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: Dyovouniotis besieged Mendenitsa (Bodonitsa) from 8 April 1821; the garrison, short of food, surrendered five days later.

name: Levidi
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Λεβιδίου (title and date); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: A sortie from Tripolitsa burned much of the village but could not take the defenders' fortified houses and withdrew. Greek local tradition counts it as a successful defence. el.wikipedia (14 April 1821): the first Greek victory in the operations around Tripolitsa.

name: Patratziki
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Πατρατζικίου (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: the Greeks withdrew from Ypati by night without result.

name: Vogortsa
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Βογόρτσας (title and date); en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris
note: el.wikipedia: night of 18 April 1821, a Souliote victory.

name: Tripolitsa (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa; el.wikipedia Πολιορκία και άλωση της Τριπολιτσάς; Trikoupis vol. 1; Finlay vol. 1; Gordon, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 1
note: Taken by storm on 23 September (O.S.) and followed by a massacre of the Muslim and Jewish population. The named battles fought during the siege (Levidi, Valtetsi, Doliana and Vervena, Grana) are separate entries.

name: Alamana
place: Alamana bridge on the Spercheios, near Thermopylae, Phthiotis
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Alamana; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Αλαμάνας; Hellenic Army General Staff (army.gr, 23 April 2025); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: Diakos was impaled at Lamia on 24 April. Some Greek sources date the battle to 23 April.

name: Acrocorinth (siege, 1821–1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία του Ακροκορίνθου (1821) (title and start date); Finlay vol. 1
note: The garrison capitulated in January 1822. el.wikipedia has separate articles for the sieges of 1822 (Dramali's relief) and 1823.

name: Acropolis (siege, 1821)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία των Αθηνών (1821) (title and dates); en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1821–1822)
note: The first siege, ended when Omer Vrioni and Omer Bey of Karystos relieved the garrison and re-entered Athens on 20 July. en.wikipedia treats this and the renewed siege as one siege (25 April 1821 – 9 June 1822, Greek victory). Here they are split to follow el.wikipedia and the opposite results.

name: Athens (1821)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Αθήνας (1821) (title and dates); en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1821–1822)
note: Armed Atticans broke into the town; the Muslims withdrew to the Acropolis.

name: Galați
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Galați (1821); el.wikipedia Μάχη του Γαλατσίου (title and dates)
note: About 600 Eterists held a fortified line against about 5,000 Ottomans. Some 20 survivors, including Karpenisiotis, broke out, and the town was sacked. Not to be confused with the Eterist rising and massacre of local Turks at Galați on 21–22 February 1821, which was not a battle.

name: Gravia Inn
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gravia Inn; el.wikipedia Μάχη στο Χάνι της Γραβιάς; Hellenic Army General Staff (army.gr); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: About 120 men held the inn against repeated assaults and heavy loss to the Ottomans, then slipped away at night before artillery arrived. en.wikipedia calls the result ambiguous; it is usually counted as a Greek victory and it checked Vrioni's march on the Peloponnese.

name: Valtetsi
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Valtetsi; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Βαλτετσίου; Trikoupis vol. 1; Kolokotronis, Διήγησις
note: Ottoman losses are given variously as 600 dead (text) and 1,149 dead and wounded (infobox) in en.wikipedia.

name: Katsarou Straits
place: Katsarou khans near Panopoulo, mountains of Elis
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Κατσαρού
note: el.wikipedia gives 27 May 1821 (30 June in the old reckoning). el.wikipedia: Giannias and his men refused to surrender and fell fighting.

name: Doliana and Vervena
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Doliana; el.wikipedia Μάχη των Δολιανών και Βερβένων; Trikoupis vol. 1
note: One entry, following el.wikipedia, which treats the two simultaneous fights as one battle: Kehaya Bey's two-pronged attack on the Greek camp at Vervena and on Nikitaras's post at Doliana, a few km apart, both repulsed. Split into two entries if the set counts them separately. Coordinates are for Doliana.

name: Methoni (siege, 1821)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Μεθώνης (title and date only)
note: Methoni (like Koroni) stayed in Ottoman hands and was resupplied by sea; it surrendered to the French only in 1828. el.wikipedia: Methoni stayed in Ottoman hands.

name: Vrachori
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Βραχωρίου (title and dates); Trikoupis vol. 1; Finlay vol. 1
note: The Muslim and Jewish garrison and population held out in their houses and towers until 11 June. The capture was followed by killings of the Muslim and Jewish inhabitants.

name: Eresos
sources: en.wikipedia Dimitrios Papanikolis; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία της Ερεσού (title and date); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: The first successful Greek fireship attack: an Ottoman two-decker (often called a 74-gun ship of the line, sometimes a frigate) at anchor off Eresos was burned. The rest of the Ottoman squadron withdrew to the Dardanelles.

name: Nucet
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη στη Μονή Νοτσέτου (title and dates only)
note: el.wikipedia: 27 May 1821; the Ottoman attack on the monastery was repulsed (Ioannis Kolokotronis, Gerasimos Orfanos, Archimandrite Servos); the Greeks withdrew that night.

name: Koltsi
place: Mount Koltsi, on the Wallachia–Transylvania border
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Κόλτσι
borderline: small action; site uncertain
note: Greek and Serb fighters under Archimandrite Servos fought their way past Ottoman troops into Austrian territory after Drăgășani.

name: Derviziana
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη στα Δερβίζιανα (title and date); en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris
note: According to en.wikipedia, Botsaris used a planned ambush to destroy a regiment of Ottoman troops from Macedonia in Hurshid Pasha's army.

name: Drăgășani
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Drăgășani; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Δραγατσανίου; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; Trikoupis vol. 1
note: Karavias's premature attack led to the destruction of the Sacred Band (Ιερός Λόχος). Ypsilantis then retreated into Austrian territory.

name: Thessaloniki (1821)
place: Near the present American Farm School, between Thermi and Thessaloniki
sources: en.wikipedia Stamos Kapsas (after Papaoikonomou, Prosopografia Agoniston tou 1821 apo ti Chalkidiki kai ti Thessaloniki, 2016); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Θεσσαλονίκης (title/date); en.wikipedia Stamos Kapsas: 'On the same day [8 June 1821], Kapsas' men confronted and defeated the Ottoman cavalry near the modern American Agricultural School, under Ahmed Bey of Giannitsa ... forcing the Ottomans to retreat to Thessaloniki' (dates in O.S.)
borderline: A cavalry clash during the rebel advance on the city; separate from Vasilika, fought two days later.
note: On 8 June 1821 O.S. the Chalkidiki rebels camped at Vasilika and Thermi to prepare an attack on Thessaloniki; that day Kapsas' men met and defeated the Ottoman cavalry of Ahmed Bey of Giannitsa near the present American Farm School and drove it back into the city.

name: Lalas
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lalas; el.wikipedia Πολιορκία και άλωση του Λάλα; Trikoupis vol. 1
note: Cephalonian volunteers under the Metaxas brothers took part. The Muslim Albanians of Lala and Yusuf Pasha's relief force withdrew to Patras on 14 June, and Lala was burned.

name: Vasilika (Thessaloniki)
place: Vasilika and the monastery of Agia Anastasia, Thessaloniki
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Vasilika (Thessaloniki); el.wikipedia Μάχη των Βασιλικών Θεσσαλονίκης; en.wikipedia Emmanouel Pappas
note: Kapsas and his men fought to the end. The defeat opened Chalkidiki to Bayram Pasha's army.

name: Rentina
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Rentina pass, June 1821); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Ρεντίνας (title and date)
note: en.wikipedia states only that the Chalkidiki rebels were defeated at the Rentina pass in June 1821, without naming commanders.

name: Sculeni
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sculeni; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Σκουλενίου (title); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: About 400–500 Eterists faced some 5,000 Ottomans with their backs to the Prut. About a quarter escaped by swimming to Russian Bessarabia. en.wikipedia's infobox also lists Olympios and Pharmakis, who were not at Sculeni.

name: Roustika
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Ρουστίκων (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: also called the battle of Zouridi, 16/17 June (or July) 1821, a Greek victory.

name: Makrynoros (1821)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη στο Μακρυνόρος (title and date only)
note: el.wikipedia: decisive Greek victory of c. 100 men under Gogos Bakolas over c. 4,000 under Ismail Pliassa; the article gives 18 June 1821 in its infobox and 18 June 1822 in its text.

name: Kydonies
sources: el.wikipedia Καταστροφή των Κυδωνιών (title)
borderline: Mainly the sack of a Greek town. It is included because the townsmen and men landed from the Greek squadron fought the Ottoman troops while the population was evacuated by sea.
note: Usually dated 2–3 June 1821 (O.S.), just after Eresos, when Tombazis's squadron was off Kydonies; the timeline copy of el.wikipedia's date reads 4 July, so the exact day is unconfirmed. The town was burned.

name: Variades
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Βαριάδων (title and date); en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris
note: el.wikipedia: the Souliotes took Variades on 14 July 1821 and razed the Ottoman fortifications.

name: Vrysakia
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Βρυσακίων (title and date); Trikoupis vol. 1
note: A victory of the Euboean rebels over the Ottoman forces of Euboea.

name: Stavros (Theodoriana)
place: Stavros, between Vourgareli and Theodoriana, Arta
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Σταυρού; Μάχη του Βουργαρελίου
note: About 5,000 Turks marched out of Arta; with reinforcements the Greeks drove them back with heavy losses. el.wikipedia also has a separate article on the battle of Vourgareli at the same place, treated here as the same action.

name: Grana
place: The trench (Grana) on Loukas hill, near Tripolitsa, Arcadia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Trench (1821); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Γράνας; en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa
note: Known in English as the Battle of the Trench. A dawn sortie of about 3,000 from Tripolitsa was routed at the trench dug to stop its foraging (about 400 Ottoman dead).

name: Vasilika
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Vasilika; el.wikipedia Μάχη των Βασιλικών Φθιώτιδας; Trikoupis vol. 1
note: A relief army marching to Omer Vrioni and the Peloponnese was destroyed (about 700 dead, 7 cannon taken). Vrioni then left Attica.

date: September 1821; explosion 8 September (O.S.; 20 September N.S.), surrender of Pharmakis 22 September (O.S.; 4 October N.S.)
name: Secu Monastery
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Μονής Σέκκου (title and date); en.wikipedia Battle of Sculeni; en.wikipedia Giorgakis Olympios; en.wikipedia Yiannis Pharmakis; National Historical Museum, Athens (item 9619)
note: Olympios blew up the powder store rather than surrender. Pharmakis held out about two more weeks and surrendered on a promise of amnesty, then was executed in Constantinople. It was the last action of the Eterist campaign.

name: Pente Pigadia (1821)
place: Pente Pigadia pass, Ioannina–Arta road, Epirus
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Πέντε Πηγαδιών (title and dates); en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris
note: el.wikipedia: a Souliote victory at the Pente Pigadia junction (Kleisoura, Preveza). Distinct from the December 1820 action.

name: Galaxidi
sources: el.wikipedia Καταστροφή του Γαλαξειδίου (title and dates); en.wikipedia Siege of Tripolitsa (19 September)
note: en.wikipedia (Siege of Tripolitsa) dates the attack to 19 September. Dozens of Galaxidiot ships were captured or burned.

name: Kassandra
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Vasilika (Thessaloniki); en.wikipedia Emmanouel Pappas; en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Κασσάνδρας (title and date)
note: About 14,000 Ottomans stormed the fortified wall at Potidaea, then sacked Kassandra. Pappas escaped by sea and died on the way to Hydra. The revolt in Chalkidiki ended, and Mount Athos capitulated without a battle.

name: Arta (siege, 1821)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Άρτας (title and dates); en.wikipedia Souliotes; en.wikipedia Markos Botsaris
note: The allies took and plundered most of the town (en.wikipedia) but not the castle. The Muslim Albanians broke with the Greeks after news of the killings at Tripolitsa, and the Greeks withdrew; scored on the failed siege. Hurshid Pasha then counter-attacked.

name: Acropolis (siege, 1821–1822)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1821–1822); el.wikipedia Άλωση της Ακρόπολης (10 June 1822)
note: The siege was renewed after Omer Vrioni left Attica in autumn 1821; the start month is approximate. The garrison capitulated on 9/10 June 1822 (O.S.), after which many of those who surrendered were killed. This is the same event as el.wikipedia's 'Άλωση της Ακρόπολης'; the 1822 batch should not list it again.

name: Styra
place: Styra, Euboea (Agios Vasileios and the Kokkinomylos windmill)
sources: IMOPH, Η μάχη των Στύρων (2021); en.wikipedia Ilias Mavromichalis; Trikoupis vol. 2; imoph.org 'Η μάχη των Στύρων' ('στὶς 12 Ἰανουαρίου τοῦ 1822'; 'Ἧττα τῶν ἑλληνικῶν δυνάμεων στὰ Στύρα'); en.wikipedia Ilias Mavromichalis (died at Styra, 12 January 1822)
note: Ilias Mavromichalis landed at Aliveri with about 600 Maniots on 5 January and marched on Styra; he first beat the Ottomans at Agios Vasileios and besieged Styra, but Omer Bey of Karystos outflanked and surrounded the Greeks, most of whom fled; Mavromichalis held out in the Kokkinomylos windmill with seven men until killed. Omer sent his head to the Sultan.

name: Dovra monastery
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Μονής Δοβράς (title only)
note: el.wikipedia: a Greek attack from Dovra monastery near Veroia during the Naousa revolt that failed, though it alarmed the Turks of the town.

name: Patras (siege 1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Πάτρας (1822); en.wikipedia Siege of Patras (1821); Kolokotronis, Διήγησις συμβάντων
note: Renewed Greek siege of the Patras citadel after the 1821 siege; the garrison held and the siege was given up when Dramali invaded in July 1822. The battle of Gerokomeio is a separate entry.

date: February 1822 (en.wikipedia; some Greek accounts give March 1822)
name: Gerokomeio
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Γηροκομείου; en.wikipedia Siege of Patras (1821)
note: Greek victory over a sortie of the Patras garrison, after which Kolokotronis renewed the siege. Exact day unverified.

name: Patras (sea)
sources: el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία της Πάτρας (1822); navalhistory.gr; Eleftheros Typos, Οι μεγάλες ναυμαχίες της Επανάστασης του 1821; Trikoupis vol. 2
note: First Greek fleet action fought in line (5½ hours). The Ottoman fleet, which had brought reinforcements to Patras, withdrew to Zakynthos; Greek sources call it a victory, some historians indecisive. navalhistory.gr dates it 26 February.

name: Saravali
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Σαραβαλίου
note: During the first siege of Patras.

name: Chios (1822)
sources: Trikoupis vol. 2; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution; en.wikipedia Chios massacre
borderline: Fighting was limited: a Samian landing and a loose siege of the castle, then brief resistance to the Ottoman landing of 11 April (N.S.); the massacre that followed is excluded
note: The Samian landing (Logothetis, Bournias) besieged the Ottoman garrison in the castle; the Kapudan Pasha's fleet landed troops on 30 March/11 April and the revolt collapsed.

name: Naousa (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Naousa massacre; el.wikipedia Καταστροφή της Νάουσας; Vakalopoulos, Ιστορία της Μακεδονίας
note: Assaults on 16–19 March and bombardment from 24 March (O.S. dates as in Greek accounts; en.wikipedia gives them without calendar). The town was stormed and a massacre followed, ending the revolt in central Macedonia.

name: Dyo Vouna (Euboea)
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στα Δυο Βουνά Ευβοίας (1822)
note: An Ottoman victory; Angelis Govios fell.

name: Kolindros
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; Vakalopoulos, Ιστορία της Μακεδονίας; Kasomoulis, Ενθυμήματα στρατιωτικά
note: Part of Mehmed Emin's suppression of the Olympus–Vermio revolt of 1822.

name: Kastania
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence; Vakalopoulos, Ιστορία της Μακεδονίας
note: Site taken as Kastania on Mt Vermio; it may be Kastania in Pieria. Preceded the siege of Naousa.

name: Kastellos (Rethymno)
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Καστέλλου Ρεθύμνης

name: Mylopotamos (Crete)
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στον Μυλοπόταμο (Κρήτης)

name: Malevizi
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Μαλεβίζι
note: The Turks were shut up in Heraklion afterwards.

name: Chalandritsa
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη της Χαλανδρίτσας; en.wikipedia Battle of Chalandritsa

name: Souli (1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη στο Ναβαρίκο, Χώνια και Κιάφα (1822); en.wikipedia Souliotes; Battle of Peta
note: About 2,000 Souliotes repelled an Ottoman army of c. 15,000; Souli nevertheless capitulated after Peta (July 1822) and was evacuated in September. Exact day unverified.

name: Chesme (1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία του Τσεσμέ (1822) (title only)

name: Tsoukalaria
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στα Τσουκαλαριά
note: c. 2,000 Greeks against c. 12,000 Turks; a Turkish victory after the first Greek success at Malaxa.

name: Chios (fireship attack)
name_el: Πυρπόληση της τουρκικής ναυαρχίδας στη Χίο
sources: Trikoupis vol. 2; en.wikipedia Konstantinos Kanaris, Chios massacre; el.wikipedia Πυρπόληση Τουρκικής Ναυαρχίδας στη Χίο (1822)
note: Kanaris burned the 84-gun flagship Mansur al-Liwa during the Bayram festivities; about 2,000 died, including the Kapudan Pasha.

name: Kompoti
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kompoti; Trikoupis vol. 2
note: Prelude to Peta; Greek victory over Ottoman cavalry from Arta. en.wikipedia gives 10 June 1822 without calendar (O.S. assumed).

name: Splantza
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη της Σπλάντζας
note: Both sides withdrew; el.wikipedia calls it a Greek success but says it can be seen as an Ottoman one, since the Greek march was stopped.

name: Peta
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Peta; Trikoupis vol. 2; St Clair, That Greece Might Still Be Free; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Πέτα
note: Defeat blamed on Gogos Bakolas abandoning his position; the Philhellene Battalion was destroyed (c. 67 killed).

name: Argos (Larissa castle)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dervenakia, Mahmud Dramali Pasha; Trikoupis vol. 2; Fotakos, Απομνημονεύματα
note: About 700 Greeks held the castle for twelve days, delaying Dramali while Kolokotronis seized the passes, then broke out at night for lack of water; the Ottomans occupied the empty castle. Greek accounts treat it as a successful defence.

name: Dervenakia
sources: Trikoupis vol. 2; Kolokotronis, Διήγησις; en.wikipedia Battle of Dervenakia; el.wikipedia Μάχη των Δερβενακίων
note: Includes the ambushes at Agios Sostis and Agios Vasileios (Nikitaras 'Tourkofagos'). en.wikipedia gives 6–8 August N.S.; 26 July O.S. = 7 August N.S. Dramali's second attempt via Agionori is a separate entry.

name: Agionori
place: Agionori and the Kleisoura defile, Corinthia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Agionori; Trikoupis vol. 2
note: Dramali broke through to Corinth with his bodyguard but lost 600–1,000 men and his baggage. The fighting in the Kleisoura defile on the Agionori road is included here.

name: Aetos
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Αετού

name: Kiato
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Κιάτου
note: Against the remnants of Dramali's army after Dervenakia.

name: Sklavokampos
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στον Σκλαβόκαμπο
note: The Turkish force retreated towards Knossos.

name: Spetses (1822)
place: Strait between Spetses and the Argolid, Argolic Gulf
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Nauplia (1822); navalhistory.gr; ellinoistorin.gr; el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία των Σπετσών
note: Also called the battle of Nauplia or of the Argolic Gulf. The Ottoman-Egyptian fleet (84 ships, with Barbary contingents) failed to relieve Nafplio and withdrew; includes the indecisive clash off Spetsopoula on 12/24 September.

name: Dadi
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Δαδίου

name: Missolonghi (first siege)
sources: en.wikipedia First siege of Missolonghi; Trikoupis vol. 2; el.wikipedia Πρώτη πολιορκία του Μεσολογγίου
note: The main Ottoman assault on Christmas night (24/25 December O.S. = 5/6 January 1823 N.S.) was repulsed; more than 500 Ottoman troops drowned crossing the Achelous in the retreat.

name: Tenedos (fireship attack)
sources: en.wikipedia Konstantinos Kanaris; el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία της Τενέδου (1822); Trikoupis vol. 2
note: Kanaris burned the Kapudan Bey's ship of the line at anchor off Tenedos; the Ottoman fleet withdrew into the Dardanelles.

name: Palamidi (capture)
sources: Trikoupis vol. 2; Kolokotronis, Διήγησις; en.wikipedia Battle of Nauplia (1822)
note: Nafplio town surrendered on 3/15 December 1822, ending the siege begun in 1821 (separate entry).

name: Plaka (1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Πλάκας (title only)
note: el.wikipedia: an attempt to relieve Souli after Kompoti (10 June 1822); the revolutionaries prevailed but did not exploit the victory.

name: Malaxa (1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Μαλάξας (1822) (title only)
note: el.wikipedia: June 1822; after an initial Greek success the Turks won on 13 or 14 June.

name: Karystos (siege 1822)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία της Καρύστου (1822) (title only)
note: Greek attempt on the Ottoman stronghold of southern Euboea, followed by the battle of Styra. el.wikipedia: the Greeks won the battle and the Ottomans fell back into the fortress; Androutsos was then ordered to leave Euboea.

name: Tympaki
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Τυμπάκι

name: Akrata
sources: en.wikipedia Andreas Londos; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Ακράτας; Trikoupis vol. 2
note: Some 3,000–4,000 Ottoman troops marching from Corinth to Patras along the coast were surrounded and destroyed; few escaped on ships sent by Yusuf Pasha.

name: Agios Vlasios
sources: en.wikipedia Georgios Karaiskakis; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αγίου Βλασίου (Αιτωλοακαρνανία)
note: Karaiskakis attacked c. 3,000 Ottoman troops retreating through Agrafa after the failed first siege of Missolonghi. Exact site unverified (en.wikipedia: 'Agios Vlasios pass, Agrafa').

name: Lechaio (1823)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Λεχαίου (1823) (title only)
note: el.wikipedia: an Ottoman attempt to resupply besieged Acrocorinth was beaten off.

name: Karpenisi
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Karpenisi, Markos Botsaris; Trikoupis vol. 3; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Καρπενησίου
note: Night attack by c. 350–450 Souliotes (of c. 1,200) on the Albanian vanguard camp; heavy Ottoman losses and booty, but Botsaris was killed and the Greeks withdrew. en.wikipedia rates it inconclusive; Greek historiography a victory.

name: Amourgelles
sources: en.wikipedia Emmanouil Tombazis, Greek War of Independence; Detorakis, History of Crete
note: About 3,000 Cretans assembled at Gergeri were defeated by the Egyptian army, losing c. 300. The 20 August date is taken as O.S. Village sited in Minoa Pediada (Heraklion), location approximate.

name: Kaliakouda
sources: en.wikipedia Second siege of Missolonghi (Mount Kaliakouda action, 29 August 1823); el.wikipedia Μάχη του Κεφαλόβρυσου
borderline: Identification of el.wikipedia's 'Μάχη του Κεφαλόβρυσου' with the Kaliakouda action is probable but unverified
note: el.wikipedia: the battle of Kaliakouda, 28 August 1823 (O.S.), on the mountain of that name in Evrytania; an Ottoman victory. Not the night attack at Kefalovryso where Botsaris died, which is the battle of Karpenisi.

name: Anatolikon (siege 1823)
sources: en.wikipedia Second siege of Missolonghi; Trikoupis vol. 3
note: English Wikipedia calls it the Second siege of Missolonghi; the Ottoman effort centred on bombarding and assaulting Anatolikon, which held. Source dates taken as O.S. (en.wikipedia text also gives 20 November for the lifting).

name: Nafplio (siege 1824)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek civil wars of 1823–1825; Trikoupis vol. 3
borderline: Blockade with skirmishes; ended by negotiated surrender
note: First civil war. Panos Kolokotronis surrendered Nafplio to Londos and Zaimis in June 1824 after his father's submission.

date: from 3 April 1824 (22 March O.S.), about two weeks
name: Tripolitsa (siege 1824)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek civil wars of 1823–1825; Trikoupis vol. 3
note: First civil war. About two weeks of fighting ended by agreement; Kolokotronis left the city and the old executive was dissolved. The first civil war formally ended on 22 May 1824 (O.S.).

name: Koutsi
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Κούτσι
note: A government victory in the first phase of the civil war.

name: Kasos
sources: en.wikipedia Kasos massacre; ellinoistorin.gr
note: Two days of bombardment and artillery duels, then a night landing by c. 1,500 Albanians; resistance at the batteries was overcome and a massacre and enslavements followed. Commemorated on 7 June (O.S.). Naval bombardment folded in.

name: Psara
sources: en.wikipedia Destruction of Psara; Trikoupis vol. 3; el.wikipedia Καταστροφή των Ψαρών
note: Amphibious assault; the last defenders of Palaiokastro (Mavri Rachi) blew up the powder magazine. Most of the population was killed or enslaved.

name: Marathon (1824)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη στον Μαραθώνα (1824) (title only)
note: el.wikipedia: at Oinoe in the plain of Marathon; Gouras held a fortified position until Evmorfopoulos arrived, then the Greeks sallied and won.

date: 17 August 1824 (5 August O.S.), after clashes from late July
name: Samos (1824)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Samos; greekcitytimes.com; navalhistory.gr; el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία της Σάμου
note: Also called the battle of Mykale or of Eptastadio (the Samos–Mycale strait). Kanaris' fireship blew up a 54-gun frigate; a Tunisian brig and a Tripolitan corvette were also destroyed and the landing on Samos was abandoned.

date: 5 September 1824 (24 August O.S.) and following days
name: Kos (1824)
sources: el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία της Κω (title); ellinoistorin.gr; navalhistory.gr; orthodoxianewsagency.gr
note: First clash after the Ottoman and Egyptian fleets joined; indecisive, five days before Gerontas.

name: Gerontas
place: Gulf of Gerontas, off Cape Posidi opposite Leros
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Gerontas; el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία του Γέροντα; orthodoxianewsagency.gr; ellinoistorin.gr
note: Fireships destroyed a 44-gun Egyptian frigate and a brig; the allied fleet withdrew to Bodrum and Samos was saved. ellinoistorin.gr dates it 28 August O.S.

name: Chios Strait (1824)
place: Between Chios, Lesbos and the Karaburun peninsula
sources: HuffPost Greece, 'Ανδρέας Μιαούλης ... οι ναυμαχίες του 1824 στο Αιγαίο'
note: Greek fireships destroyed a 12-gun vessel and a 20-gun corvette at night and the Ottoman fleet withdrew to Mytilene; sometimes called the action off Mytilene. The source gives 24 September without calendar (O.S. assumed).

name: Roumeliot campaign in the Peloponnese
sources: el.wikipedia Εκστρατεία Ρουμελιωτών στην Πελοπόννησο (εμφύλια σύγκρουση); en.wikipedia Greek civil wars of 1823–1825
borderline: A campaign of several clashes rather than one named battle
note: Second civil war: Panos Kolokotronis was killed near Tripolitsa (13/25 November 1824); Gouras occupied Corinth (23 November/5 December); Karaiskakis and Tzavelas drove Londos and Zaimis out of Achaea; Kolokotronis and his allies were arrested in January 1825.

name: Schinolakka
sources: Kargakos, Η Ελληνική Επανάσταση του 1821, vol. 2, ch. 24 (Η μάχη της Σχινόλακκας, 15 Μαρτίου 1825); imoph.org anniversary note 'Μάχη Σχινόλακκας' (citing Karatasos' report)
note: Egyptian regulars attacked about 200 Macedonians under Karatasos holding the village, about 1.5 hours from Neokastro; reinforced by other Greek bands and helped by heavy afternoon rain that disabled Egyptian muskets, they held, and the Egyptians withdrew to their siege camp. Called the first Greek success against Ibrahim. Casualty claims vary (Karatasos: about 500 Egyptian dead and wounded).

name: Neokastro (siege)
sources: Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2; en.wikipedia Battle of Sphacteria (1825)
note: Ibrahim's first siege in the Morea, with Egyptian assaults and bombardment. Old Navarino (Paliokastro) surrendered for lack of water just after Sphacteria (late April/early May O.S.); the Neokastro garrison capitulated in May 1825 (c. 11/23 May; date not verified) and was allowed to leave, with chiefs kept as hostages. Schinolakka and Kremmydi, fought during the siege, are separate entries.

name: Kremmydi
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kremmydi; Kargakos, Η Ελληνική Επανάσταση του 1821, vol. 2, ch. 24 (Μάχη στο Κρεμμύδι, 7 Απριλίου 1825); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: The main Greek army (figures vary from 3,000 to 7,000) tried to relieve Neokastro; it was routed by a frontal infantry attack combined with a cavalry flank attack, losing over 500 killed.

name: Missolonghi (third siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kasomoulis, Ενθυμήματα στρατιωτικά; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 30–31
note: Numbered the second siege by Greek writers such as Kargakos. Includes mine warfare, sorties and the repulse of the Egyptian assaults of February 1826. Vasiladi, Klisova, the Exodus and Miaoulis' relief actions (Skrofes, Dragamestos, Cape Papas) are separate entries.

name: Sphacteria
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sphacteria (1825); Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 24 (Η μάχη της Σφακτηρίας; Η έξοδος του «Άρεως»); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: Combined land and sea action: about 1,500 Egyptians landed from the fleet and overran the island garrison (about 350 Greeks killed). In the bay the Hydriot brig Ares (Nikolaos Votsis) fought its way out through the Egyptian fleet carrying Mavrokordatos; other Greek ships escaped.

name: Modon (fireship attack)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sphacteria (1825); en.wikipedia Andreas Miaoulis; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 26 (επιχείρηση κατά της Μεθώνης); Gordon, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: Greek fireships sent into the harbour burned an Egyptian frigate and many smaller warships and transports (en.wikipedia: 12 vessels; figures vary). It did not save Neokastro or stop Ibrahim's supply.

name: Cape Kafireas
place: Channel between Cape Kafireas (Cavo Doro), Euboea, and Andros
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 26 (Η ναυμαχία του Καφηρέα, 20 Μαΐου); Argolic Library article 'Η Ναυμαχία του Καφηρέα και η θυσία του Επιδαύριου πυρπολητή'; Gordon, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: The Ottoman fleet sailing from the Dardanelles to support the western sieges was attacked with fireships; Greek accounts report Ottoman warships burned (a frigate in Greek tradition) and the self-sacrifice of a fireship captain from Epidaurus, but the fleet went on to Souda. Commander as in general accounts; possibly the same action some lists call the battle off Andros.

name: Maniaki
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Maniaki; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 24 (Η μάχη στο Μανιάκι, 20 Μαΐου 1825); greece2021.gr timeline
note: Papaflessas' force shrank by desertion from about 3,000 to under 1,000 before Ibrahim attacked with over 6,000; almost all the defenders were killed. Finlay's '1 June' is the New Style date of the same day.

name: Trikorfa (1825)
place: Trikorfa heights, west of Tripolitsa, Arcadia
sources: task checklist (Greek Wikipedia); cf. Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 25 (Μάχες γύρω από την Τρίπολη)
note: el.wikipedia: near Tripolitsa; Ibrahim won and the Greeks lost about 200 men.

name: Lerna Mills
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Lerna Mills; Makrygiannis, Απομνημονεύματα; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 24 (Η μάχη των Μύλων, 13 Ιουνίου 1825)
note: About 350 Greeks with two gunboats held the walled mills against some 5,000 Egyptians; Ibrahim gave up the march on Nafplio and returned to Tripolitsa. The first clear Greek victory over Ibrahim's main army.

date: June 1825, just before Ibrahim entered Tripolitsa on 11/23 June
name: Drampala
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 24 (Η μάχη της Δραμπάλας – Κατάληψη Τριπολιτσάς); Kolokotronis, Διήγησις συμβάντων
note: Kolokotronis' attempt to bar Ibrahim's road to Tripolitsa failed, and Ibrahim occupied the abandoned, partly burned town on 11/23 June 1825. Site identification approximate.

name: Skrofes
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 30 (Η ναυμαχία στις Σκρόφες, 23 Ιουλίου 1825); en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: Miaoulis' fleet attacked the Ottoman fleet blockading Missolonghi, drove it off and got supplies into the town.

name: Alexandria (1825)
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 26 (εκστρατεία κατά της Αλεξάνδρειας); Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2; Gordon, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: Kanaris' fireships entered the harbour to burn the fleet being fitted out for Ibrahim; the wind dropped and the attack failed, and Egyptian warships chased the Greeks off.

name: Kakosalesi
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Κακοσάλεσι; en.wikipedia Battle of Kakosalesi

name: Vartholomio
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Βαρθολομιού
note: Against Ibrahim's forces; indecisive, the fighting was broken off.

name: Vasiladi
sources: en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: About 1,000 Egyptians in flat boats stormed the fortified islet held by 61 men after a day's fighting; Dolmas, the islet of Poros and Anatoliko surrendered in the following days, closing the lagoon to Greek supply.

name: Karystos (1826)
sources: Gordon, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: Fabvier's new regular corps, with irregulars, landed to take Karystos; after fighting the garrison and Ottoman relief forces it had to re-embark.

name: Klisova
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kleisova; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 31
note: About 130 defenders beat off six attacks by Kütahı's Albanians (Kütahı wounded) and then three Egyptian battalions under Hussein Bey, who was killed. A celebrated victory that did not change the fate of Missolonghi.

name: Exodus of Missolonghi
place: Missolonghi and the slopes of Mount Zygos (Agios Symeon)
sources: en.wikipedia Third siege of Missolonghi; Kasomoulis, Ενθυμήματα στρατιωτικά; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 31
note: Breakout of the starving garrison and population: of some 7,000–9,000 who tried, about 1,000–2,000 reached safety. Kapsalis and Bishop Joseph died blowing up the powder stores; the town fell on Palm Sunday. The relief attack promised by Karaiskakis did not come.

name: Kastraki
place: Kastraki on Mount Helmos, near Solos, Kalavryta, Achaea
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kastraki
note: Ibrahim, marching from Missolonghi to Tripolitsa, stormed a fortified refuge sheltering thousands of civilians of the Kalavryta villages; hundreds were killed or fell from the cliff and about 1,000 captured. en.wikipedia gives 5 May, taken here as Old Style.

name: Varnakova (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of Varnakova
note: About 150 men sent by Karaiskakis held the monastery for six days against some 4,000 Ottomans and Albanians, then withdrew; the monastery was blown up. en.wikipedia gives 20–26 May, taken here as Old Style.

name: Verga
place: Verga wall near Almyros, Messenian Mani
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman–Egyptian invasion of Mani; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 33 (Μάχη της Βέργας, 22 Ιουνίου 1826); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: About 7,000 Egyptians, supported by ships firing from the sea, assaulted the fortified line held by some 2,000 Maniots and refugees and were repulsed eight times; Ibrahim withdrew when Kolokotronis threatened his rear. Egyptian losses claimed up to 2,500. en.wikipedia gives 21 June for the start of the attack.

name: Diros
place: Bay of Diros, near Areopoli (Tsimova), Mani
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman–Egyptian invasion of Mani; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 33 (Η μάχη του Διρού); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: About 1,500 Egyptians landed to take Tsimova from the rear while Verga was attacked; they were driven back to the ships with heavy loss (about 1,000). The part of the women is remembered ('the Amazons of Diros'). The landing is dated 23 or 24 June O.S.

name: Mehmetaga
sources: protothema.gr, 'Η νίκη των Ελλήνων επί του Ιμπραήμ στο Μεχμέταγα (Ιούλιος 1826)'; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: Night attack that seized the Egyptian post at Mehmetaga; about 200 Egyptians reported killed and Egyptian reinforcements from Tripolitsa withdrew. The tower was later besieged and blown up by Ibrahim. Site identification approximate.

name: Acropolis (siege, 1826–27)
sources: en.wikipedia Siege of the Acropolis (1826–1827); Makrygiannis, Απομνημονεύματα; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 33–35
note: Kütahı invested Athens in the summer of 1826 and took the lower town in August; Gouras was killed on the walls in the autumn and Fabvier broke in with men and powder in December 1826. The relief battles (Chaidari, Kamatero, Kastella, Keratsini, Agios Spyridon, Phaleron) are separate entries; the garrison capitulated a month after Phaleron. Exact start date not verified (en.wikipedia infobox read as 25 June/August 1826 O.S.).

name: Chaidari
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 34 (Μάχη Χαϊδαρίου, 6–8 Αυγούστου 1826); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: First attempt to relieve the Acropolis: Kütahı's attack on the Greek camp was beaten off, Fabvier's regulars holding in square, but quarrels between Karaiskakis and Fabvier and lack of supplies made the Greeks withdraw and the siege went on; some accounts call it an Ottoman success.

name: Polyaravos
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman–Egyptian invasion of Mani; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 33 (Β΄ φάση – Μάχη Πολυαράβου)
note: Ibrahim's second thrust into Mani, from Laconia, was held up at the Stathakos tower near Kariopoli and then thrown back at Polyaravos by a Maniot sally; his last attempt on Mani. Strength figures conflict (4,000 or 8,000 Egyptians).

name: Arachova
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Arachova; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 34; greece2021.gr timeline
note: Mustafa Bey's force of about 2,000 was surrounded in Arachova in snow; relief failed and its breakout on the last day was destroyed (about 1,700 killed, Greek losses slight). Karaiskakis built a trophy of heads. en.wikipedia states 18–24 November as New Style, but these are the Old Style dates of Greek historiography. Preceded by Karaiskakis' siege of Domvraina (27 October – 14 November O.S.).

name: Tourkochori
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Τουρκοχώρι
note: After Arachova, a body of 700 under Mehmed Pasha was beaten.

name: Distomo (1827)
sources: task checklist (Greek Wikipedia); cf. Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 35 (Karaiskakis' successes, 1827)
note: el.wikipedia: a Greek victory over a larger force under Omer Pasha of Karystos.

name: Kamatero
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kamatero; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Makrygiannis, Απομνημονεύματα
note: A relief force of about 3,500 camped at Kamatero was broken by Ottoman cavalry and artillery; 300–500 Greeks were killed, among them the French philhellene Bourbaki, whose head was sent to the Sultan. Trikoupis blames Bourbaki, Makrygiannis Mavrovouniotis.

name: Treis Pyrgoi
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη των Τριών Πύργων
note: A heavy Greek defeat (c. 300 dead) in the campaign to relieve the Acropolis.

name: Kastella
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kamatero (Gordon fortifying Munychia); Gordon, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: Gordon landed at Piraeus, seized and fortified Munychia and held it against Ottoman attacks, giving the Greeks a base for the relief of the Acropolis.

name: Keratsini
sources: greece2021.gr timeline 'Μάχη στο Κερατσίνι' (placed between Arachova and June 1827); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: Kütahı attacked Karaiskakis' newly fortified camp at Keratsini and was repulsed with loss.

name: Oropos (1827)
sources: eefshp.org article on Karteria; en.wikipedia Frank Abney Hastings; eefshp.org/en/?p=14724 (Oropos, March 1827: 'neutralized the Turkish fort and blew up its gunpowder depot', two cargo ships seized); en.wikipedia Frank Abney Hastings ('Oropos and Volos in March and April 1827')
borderline: A raid by the steam warship Karteria (shore bombardment and capture of ships), not a battle with a standard name.
note: Karteria anchored about 200 m off the Ottoman fort at Oropos, the supply base of Kütahı's army besieging the Acropolis, silenced it with continuous fire and blew up its powder magazine, and took two cargo ships that had come from Euboea; she then withdrew to Aegina as Ottoman reinforcements arrived.

name: Volos (1827)
sources: eefshp.org article on Karteria; en.wikipedia Frank Abney Hastings; eefshp.org/en/?p=14724 (Volos, 8 April 1827: 300 shells over about four hours, depots and fortifications destroyed, most Turkish ships sunk, four cargo ships captured); en.wikipedia Frank Abney Hastings
borderline: A raid by the steam warship Karteria on the port of Volos, not a battle with a standard name.
note: Karteria bombarded Volos, the main Ottoman supply port of Thessaly, for about four hours (some 300 shells), destroying powder magazines and fortifications and sinking most of the Ottoman vessels in the harbour; on the way back she took four cargo ships bound for the Ottoman army.

date: April 1827 (garrison capitulated c. 15/27 April; date not verified)
name: Agios Spyridon (Piraeus)
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 35 (Μάχη Αγίου Σπυρίδωνος); en.wikipedia Georgios Karaiskakis; Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
note: The Albanian garrison of the fortified monastery surrendered under bombardment from land and sea and was massacred while marching out, despite the terms.

name: Phaleron
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Phaleron; Makrygiannis, Απομνημονεύματα; Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 35; army.gr (ΓΕΣ) commemoration
note: Night landing at Phaleron to march on the Acropolis; the advanced force was caught in the open by Ottoman cavalry and destroyed (1,500–2,000 killed), the worst Greek defeat of the war. Karaiskakis had been mortally wounded in a skirmish on 22 April/4 May and died the next day.

name: Alexandria (1827)
sources: greece2021.gr timeline 'Πυρπόληση του εχθρικού στόλου στην Αλεξάνδρεια' (placed just before the Treaty of London, July 1827); Finlay, History of the Greek Revolution, vol. 2
borderline: fireship raid with limited fighting
note: Cochrane's fireships attacked the Egyptian fleet in harbour; little was burned before the Egyptian fleet came out and the Greeks withdrew.

name: Megalo Spilaio
place: Mega Spilaio monastery, near Kalavryta, Achaea
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 35 (events in the Peloponnese: Μέγα Σπήλαιο); Trikoupis, Ιστορία της Ελληνικής Επαναστάσεως
note: Ibrahim's attack on the fortified cave monastery was repulsed.

name: Kafkaria
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 35 (Η μάχη της Καυκαριάς, 26 και 27 Αυγούστου 1827)
note: Fought during Ibrahim's 1827 campaign in the western Peloponnese. el.wikipedia (26–27 August 1827): a Greek victory.

name: Itea
place: Bay of Itea (Salona), Gulf of Corinth
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Itea; en.wikipedia Karteria; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 35 (Ναυμαχία της Ιτέας, 18 Σεπτεμβρίου 1827); eefshp.org 'The naval battle of Agali (Itea) – September 17, 1827'
note: Also called the battle of Agali. First action fought by a steam warship: the Karteria with a brig and two gunboats destroyed or captured most of an Ottoman flotilla anchored under shore batteries. Ibrahim's angry reaction contributed to the run-up to Navarino.

name: Chios (siege, 1827–28)
sources: en.wikipedia Chios expedition; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 37–38; greece2021.gr timeline 'Εκστρατεία στην Χίο'
note: Fabvier's expedition landed, drove the garrison into the castle and besieged it without a sea blockade; a Greek success against a sortie on 12 January 1828 was not decisive, and after an Ottoman squadron landed 3,000 reinforcements at the end of February the Greeks withdrew in March 1828.

name: Frangokastello
sources: en.wikipedia Greek War of Independence (Crete); en.wikipedia Hatzimichalis Dalianis; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 38 (Η μάχη στο Φραγκοκάστελλο)
note: Dalianis, who had landed with about 700 men and occupied the castle in March, was overwhelmed by some 8,000 Ottomans; he and about 385 men were killed and the castle surrendered days later. Sfakians ambushed the returning Ottomans. Origin of the Drosoulites legend. English sources mix dates (17 March, 13 May).

name: Vonitsa (siege)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Koronisia (1829) (Vonitsa Greek again on 5 March 1829); Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 39–40; castleroute.culture.gov.gr Vonitsa ('In 1828, Greek troops, led by ... Sir Richard Church, conquered the city once and for all after a battle. The Ottoman garrison, besieged in the castle, surrendered in March 1829'); en.wikipedia Battle of Koronisia (1829) ('On March 5, 1829, Vonitsa became Greek again'); IMOPH, Richard Church
borderline: start date and course of the siege not verified in this session
note: Church's forces, supported by Greek gunboats in the Ambracian Gulf, took the town and blockaded the castle, which passed to the Greeks on 5/17 March 1829, the day of Koronisia.

name: Martino
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Μαρτίνου; en.wikipedia Battle of Martino
note: About 250 Ottomans killed.

name: Koronisia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Koronisia (1829); Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 39 (Είσοδος στον Αμβρακικό – Μάχη Κορωνησίας)
note: The Souliote militia under Koutsonikas held the islet against Kütahı's attempt to cross into western Rumeli. Kargakos places the battle with the Greek entry into the Ambracian Gulf in 1828; en.wikipedia dates it 5 March 1829 (taken here as Old Style).

name: Mesovouni
place: Mesovouni, eastern Rumeli (probably Boeotia; site not identified)
sources: Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 40 (Η μάχη του Μεσοβουνίου)
note: el.wikipedia: near Thebes, during Dimitrios Ypsilantis' last campaign; a Greek victory.

name: Petra
place: Pass of Petra, between Thebes and Livadeia, Boeotia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Petra; en.wikipedia Demetrios Ypsilantis; Kargakos, vol. 2, ch. 40 (Η μάχη της Πέτρας, 12 Σεπτεμβρίου 1829); eurohoops.net/el 'Η μάχη της Πέτρας: η τελευταία σύγκρουση του αγώνα του 1821'
note: Last battle of the war: Aslan Bey's force withdrawing north was defeated and capitulated, agreeing to evacuate eastern Rumeli.

name: Poros (1831)
sources: en.wikipedia Ioannis Kapodistrias; en.wikipedia Andreas Miaoulis; Finlay, History of Greece, vol. 7
note: The Hydriot constitutionalists had seized the national fleet at Poros in July 1831. Rikord's squadron sank the corvette Spetses and the Bourtzi fort was overrun while Kallergis' regulars and irregulars attacked by land; Miaoulis blew up the frigate Hellas and the corvette Hydra rather than surrender them, and the government troops sacked Poros.

name: Provarma
sources: el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση του 1841 (after Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους, vol. ΙΓ); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841): 'they lost, having sustained heavy casualties, at the battles of Provarma, Vafe, Ksida and Vryses' (citing Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους vol. ΙΓ, pp. 81–83); revolt declared 22 February 1841
borderline: called a συμπλοκή (clash); exact site and date not established
note: One of four clashes (Provarma, Vafes, Xyda, Vryses of Pediada) in which the rebels suffered heavy losses; the revolt was over by about April 1841.

name: Vafes (1841)
sources: el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση του 1841; en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841) ('Vafe'), after Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους vol. ΙΓ
borderline: called a συμπλοκή (clash); date not established

name: Xyda
sources: el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση του 1841; en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841) ('Ksida'); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841) ('Ksida'), after Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους vol. ΙΓ
borderline: called a συμπλοκή (clash); date not established
note: Identified with the village of Xydas, renamed Lyttos.

name: Vryses (Pediada, 1841)
sources: el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση του 1841; en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1841) ('Vryses'; the leaders then fled to Greece with women and children), after Ιστορία του Ελληνικού Έθνους vol. ΙΓ
borderline: called a συμπλοκή (clash); site and date not established
note: After this defeat the leaders fled to Greece with many women and children.

name: Chalkida (1847)
sources: el.wikipedia Νικόλαος Κριεζώτης
borderline: series of clashes in an anti-government revolt, not a standard named battle
note: Kriezotis, freed by his followers, fortified himself on the shore of Chalkida and proclaimed an anti-dynastic revolt; government troops defeated him and he fled to Ottoman territory. Theodoros Grivas' simultaneous 1847 revolt in Acarnania produced no named battle found in the sources.

name: Argostoli (1848)
sources: en.wikipedia United States of the Ionian Islands; el.wikipedia Κεφαλονιά
borderline: skirmishes ('αψιμαχίες') of armed peasants with the British garrison; no standard battle name
note: The attack on the towns failed; Britain responded by restricting the press.

name: Skala (1849)
sources: en.wikipedia United States of the Ionian Islands
borderline: rural rising put down by British troops and martial law; individual clashes not named in the sources used
note: Calendar of the 15 August date not stated; ringleaders executed after the suppression.

name: Skoulikaria (January 1854)
sources: el.wikipedia Επανάσταση της Ηπείρου (1854); el.wikipedia Επανάσταση της Ηπείρου (1854) (per the batch); en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854 does not mention a January action at Skoulikaria; no other source found
borderline: described as an attack, not a named battle; commander not named in the text
note: The rebels drove the Turks back to Arta; the opening action of the revolt.

name: Arta (siege, 1854)
sources: el.wikipedia Σπυρίδων Καραϊσκάκης (επικεφαλής στην πολιορκία της Άρτας); en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854
note: en.wikipedia says Karaiskakis captured Arta with 2,500 irregulars before Ottoman troops retook it with heavy artillery; Greek sources speak of a siege. Either way the Ottomans held or regained the town.

name: Kalambaka (1854)
sources: el.wikipedia Χριστόδουλος Χατζηπέτρος, Δημήτριος Πετροπουλάκης; en.wikipedia Christodoulos Hatzipetros
note: Greek biography: about 1,000 men under Hatzipetros and Leotsakos held off 12,000 Turks all day and routed them with the sword after sunset. en.wikipedia: Hatzipetros was defeated and nearly captured near Kalambaka. Accounts conflict (possibly two separate actions).

name: Metsovo (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854; el.wikipedia Θεόδωρος Γρίβας
note: Grivas took Metsovo in early March; after repeated Ottoman attacks he withdrew on 27 March and the town was looted and partly burned.

name: Peta (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854; en.wikipedia Kitsos Tzavelas
note: en.wikipedia states the Ottomans had British and French artillery support (the Crimean War allies); after heavy losses Tzavelas retreated behind the Greek border.

name: Ormylia (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia 1854 Macedonian rebellion; el.wikipedia Μακεδονική επανάσταση του 1854
note: Karatasos attacked the Ottoman camp but a counter-attack drove him back; he was defeated again near Athos on 28 May and left on a French ship.

name: Plaka (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854
note: The Ottoman force was forced to retreat, the Albanians suffering heavy losses. Site identified with Plaka on the Arachthos (approx.).

name: Kleidi (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854; en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854: 'After a number of vicious battles in Voulgareli, Skoulikaria and in Kleidi on 12 May, the revolt was doomed and the Epirotes retreated behind the Greek border'
borderline: site not securely identified
note: After Voulgareli, Skoulikaria and Kleidi the Epirote rebels retreated behind the Greek border.

name: Spilaio (1854)
sources: el.wikipedia Θεόδωρος Ζιάκας; en.wikipedia 1854 Macedonian rebellion
note: Ziakas with about 300 men repulsed the first Ottoman assaults (en.wikipedia calls the 28 May action 'Houn Havral'), then accepted British and French mediation; armistice of 31 May and withdrawal to Greece with about 1,000 civilians.

name: Karpero (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia 1854 Macedonian rebellion; el.wikipedia Θεόδωρος Ζιάκας
note: 'A serious defeat' of the Ottoman army, immediately before the Spilaio battle.

name: Voulgareli (1854)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854; en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854 (as above)
borderline: only listed by name among the 'vicious battles' that ended the revolt

name: Skoulikaria (May 1854)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854; en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1854 (as above); an Augsburger Allgemeine Zeitung report of May 1854 (marksrussianmilitaryhistory.info) shows Skoulikaria as the rebels' fallback village after Peta
borderline: only listed by name among the battles that ended the revolt

name: Nafplion (1862)
sources: el.wikipedia Ναυπλιακή Επανάσταση, Πάνος Κορωναίος, Επανάσταση της 23ης Οκτωβρίου 1862
note: Army units in Nafplion rose against King Otto; government troops based at Corinth stormed the rebel positions on 1 March and the rebels capitulated on 24 March with an amnesty.

name: Iouniana (Athens, 1863)
sources: el.wikipedia Ιουνιανά
borderline: street fighting between army factions in the capital; may be classed as civil strife rather than a battle
note: About 200 dead; Papadiamantopoulos' attempt to seize the palace failed; fighting stopped under an ultimatum of the three protecting Powers.

date: late August 1866 (O.S.), five days after the Askyfou proclamation
name: Vryses (1866)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869 (after Detorakis, History of Crete); politistiko-rethymno.org 'Η Μεγάλη Κρητική Επανάσταση 1866-1869'
note: First major rebel victory: the Egyptian force trying to cut the road to Sfakia was besieged and retreated to Chania, abandoning its supplies. Egyptian troops fought as Ottoman vassals.

name: Almyros (1866)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
borderline: minor repulse, named only by place

name: Malaxa (1866)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Μαλάξας (disambiguation lists Μάχη της Μαλάξας (1866))
note: Mustafa's first offensive after the rebels rejected his ultimatum (Assembly of Kambi, 7 Sept).

name: Kastamonitsa (1866)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: The rebels retreated after losing 70 men.

name: Kandanos (siege, 1866)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: Kriaris took the Selino strongholds (Stavros and others) and penned the Turks in Kandanos; Mustafa relieved the garrison after Malaxa. On his return his troops were ambushed (21 Sept O.S., site not named).

name: Vafes (1866)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη στο Βαφέ, Βαφές Χανίων, Θρασύβουλος Μάνος; fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869; en.wikipedia Cretan revolt (1866–1869)
note: Cretans and philhellene volunteers fought a Turco-Egyptian force five times larger and retreated with heavy losses; the defeat demoralised the rebels and many villages submitted.

name: Keramia (1866)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869; G. Paraschos' melodrama 'Η μάχη των Κεραμειών' (cited on el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση (1866-1869))
note: During Mustafa's drive into the hills near Chania (Lakkoi, Theriso and Meskla were burned) his troops were repulsed at Aliakes and lost about 1,500 men at Keramia, forcing him back to the plain.

name: Arkadi (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Μονή Αρκαδίου, Κρητική Επανάσταση (1866-1869); en.wikipedia Arkadi Monastery; fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: About 15,000 Ottoman troops with 30 guns stormed the monastery held by 259 armed men sheltering some 700 women and children; the defenders blew up the powder magazine. About 850 of 964 inside died; Ottoman losses put at 1,500. Commemorated on 8 November.

name: Tylissos (1867)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: About 600 Ottoman soldiers reported killed.

name: Fodele (1867)
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
borderline: attack on a landing party, not a named battle
note: Petropoulakis' volunteers, landed from the Panhellenion, were attacked at once and forced into the mountains.

name: Katre (1867)
place: Katre gorge, between Krapi and Askyfou, Sfakia
sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
borderline: ambush
note: Returning from his winter campaign in Sfakia (Frangokastello), Mustafa's army was ambushed in the Katre gorge and lost about 500 men.

name: Lasithi (1867)
sources: el.wikipedia Οροπέδιο Λασιθίου; fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869; Mamalakis, 'Ο Πάνος Κορωναίος και η εκστρατεία του Ομέρ στο Λασίθι', Κρητικά Χρονικά 5 (1951)
note: Omer crossed Mount Efendis from Kastelli and broke into the plateau on 21 May after hard fighting; the plateau was ravaged and Kroustallenia monastery destroyed, but the rebels returned after he left.

name: Gergeri (1867)
