sources: fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: The Ottoman column suffered heavy losses.

name: Askyfou (1867)
sources: el.wikipedia Ασκύφου, Ασή Γωνιά Χανίων; fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: Greek local history: the Sfakians repulsed Mehmet Pasha and trapped his men at Kares until Reşid Pasha relieved them; heat and lack of water then forced the Turks to abandon Askyfou. Detorakis (via fr.wikipedia): Omer forced his way into Sfakia and burned Sfakia village before the water shortage made him withdraw. A 'fierce battle' near Asi Gonia in June 1867 belongs to the same campaign.

name: Arkadion (sea)
sources: ru.wikipedia Аркади (пароход); el.wikipedia Ένωσις (ατμόπλοιο); fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
borderline: engagement of an armed blockade-runner of the Central Committee for Crete (crewed by Greek navy sailors) rather than a named fleet battle
note: The Arkadion fought Ottoman warships, tried to ram and board the Izzeddin, then was beached, unloaded its cargo to the rebels and was burned by its crew.

name: Enosis (sea)
sources: el.wikipedia Ένωσις (ατμόπλοιο); N. Sourmelis, 'Οι εις Κρήτην είκοσι πέντε πλόες ... και η ναυμαχία της Ενώσεως' (1869); fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869
note: Ambushed by Hobart's ships, the Enosis returned fire, damaged the Izzeddin's paddle and broke through into Syros, where Hobart blockaded it. el.wikipedia dates this 2 December 1867, but the Syros blockade it describes (and fr.wikipedia) belong to December 1868, leading to the Ottoman ultimatum to Greece.

name: Kalonykti (1868)
place: Kalonykti and Valsamonero (or the Agiasmatsi tower), Rethymno
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Καλονύκτη (after Psilakis, Kriaris, Kallonas)
note: The rebels first repulsed the Ottoman detachment but withdrew to Roustika in the afternoon when superior reinforcements arrived.

name: Chainospilio (1868)
place: Chainospilio cave near Asi Gonia, Apokoronas
sources: el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση (1866-1869) ('η Προσωρινή Κυβέρνηση πολιορκήθηκε στη Γωνιά'), Ασή Γωνιά Χανίων; fr.wikipedia Révolte crétoise de 1866-1869; politistiko-rethymno.org
note: Siege of the revolutionary Provisional Government, which ended the revolt in western Crete. el.wikipedia places it at 'Gonia of Kissamos' on 11 Dec; local sources place it at the Chainospilio cave of Asi Gonia on 23 Dec (the same day in the other calendar); three Asigoniots broke out after hard fighting.

name: Plaka (1878)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1878
borderline: capture of an outpost
note: The Epirotes overcame the Ottoman outpost but retreated when 2,000 Ottoman troops arrived from Ioannina.

name: Kolindros (1878)
sources: el.wikipedia Επανάσταση του Λιτοχώρου
borderline: attack on a garrison
note: The Turks retook the area on 25 February; the bishop burned the cathedral to keep it from them.

name: Litochoro (1878)
sources: el.wikipedia Επανάσταση του Λιτοχώρου, Μακεδονική επανάσταση του 1878; en.wikipedia 1878 Macedonian rebellion
note: The Ottomans retook Litochoro, burning 9 churches and 320 houses; 2,800 rifles landed for the rebels were captured.

name: Saranda (1878)
sources: en.wikipedia Epirus Revolt of 1878
note: en.wikipedia gives 'March 4' for the end of the fighting, which sits awkwardly with its own chronology (Botsi declaration 12 March); about 20 villages of Delvina were burned afterwards.

name: Mouzaki (1878)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Μουζακίου; en.wikipedia Battle of Mouzaki
note: Irregulars supported by Greek regular troops (Greece officially uninvolved) defeated the detachment sent from Trikala. el.wikipedia Θεσσαλική Επανάσταση του 1878 says the movement failed 'after several unsuccessful battles', which are not named.

name: Vryses (1895)
sources: en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1897–1898); el.wikipedia Κρητική Επανάσταση (1895-1898), Πολιορκία του Βάμου
note: After a day-long (el.wikipedia: several-day) fight the Ottomans retreated, losing 200 men. The Vamos article lists for November 1895 the battles of Alikambos, Kares Apokoronou and Pyrgos Kefala (probably the same operations), after first clashes at Asi Gonia on 11 and 19 October (O.S.).

name: Vamos (siege)
sources: el.wikipedia Πολιορκία του Βάμου, Κρητική Επανάσταση (1895-1898); en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1897–1898)
note: About 1,400 Cretans besieged the fortified government seat and defeated the relief forces in ten days of fighting from Almyrida to Armeni, the Turks fleeing with some 800 casualties. en.wikipedia: siege 4–18 May, fort captured 18 May (calendar not stated).

name: Demir Kapija (1896)
place: Iron Gates of the Axios (Demir Kapija), Tikves
sources: el.wikipedia Μακεδονική επανάσταση του 1896
note: A battle of many hours in which the leader of the 1896 bands fell. The bands of 1896, sent in by the Ethniki Etaireia, are forerunners of the Macedonian Struggle bands.

name: Voukolies
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Βουκολιών, Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897; en.wikipedia Cretan Revolt (1897–1898), Template:Campaignbox Greco-Turkish War (1897)
note: The fort fell after a day's bombardment; the escaping garrison was ambushed by Cretan bands and the rest surrendered (c. 240 Ottoman casualties, 25 Greek). en.wikipedia dates the capture 19 February.

name: Livadeia (Crete)
place: Leivadia barracks and the olive groves west of Chania (from Monodendri hill)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Λειβαδιών; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897), International Squadron (Cretan intervention, 1897–1898)
note: The Greek battalion stormed the barracks and the Ottomans fled to Chania (c. 600 Ottoman dead, c. 100 Greek casualties); the Powers' admirals then forbade any further advance.

name: Akrotiri (Profitis Ilias)
place: Profitis Ilias hill, Akrotiri peninsula, Chania
winner_first: the Great Powers beat Cretan rebels
sources: en.wikipedia International Squadron (Cretan intervention, 1897–1898), Cretan Revolt (1897–1898)
borderline: naval bombardment of an insurgent camp by the Great Powers' fleets; the insurgents had little means of reply
note: Insurgents with Greek-army artillery took the heights east of Chania and attacked the town on 13 Feb (N.S.), repelled by Ottoman troops and bashi-bazouks; when they raised the Greek flag and refused to disperse the squadron shelled them. A military success for the Powers, but the legend of Kayales holding up the flagpole made it a Cretan symbol. French and Italian ships were present but did not fire.

name: Malaxa (Aptera blockhouse, 1897)
place: Ottoman blockhouse at Aptera on Malaxa mountain, above Souda Bay
sources: en.wikipedia International Squadron (Cretan intervention, 1897–1898), Cretan Revolt (1897–1898); el.wikipedia Μαλάξα Χανίων
note: The first attack (28 Feb) was driven off by Ottoman naval gunfire with the admirals' permission; on 25 March the insurgents captured the blockhouse but were shelled out of it by the International Squadron.

name: Kissamos (siege, 1897)
sources: en.wikipedia International Squadron (Cretan intervention, 1897–1898)
borderline: insurgent attempt to mine the fort walls, broken up by naval gunfire
note: After these March actions organised insurgent operations against Ottoman and European forces ceased.

name: Baltino (1897)
sources: el.wikipedia Εισβολή Ελλήνων ατάκτων στη Μακεδονία (1897); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897)
borderline: capture of a garrison after partial resistance
note: en.wikipedia records armed resistance at Baltino by local Aromanian fighters on the Ottoman side. The irregular raid gave the Porte its casus belli.

name: Kritades (1897)
sources: el.wikipedia Εισβολή Ελλήνων ατάκτων στη Μακεδονία (1897)
note: The last success of the irregulars (150 rifles and 25 prisoners taken; five Macedonian chieftains killed). A nizam regiment had also been repulsed at Velemitsi.

name: Krania (1897)
sources: el.wikipedia Εισβολή Ελλήνων ατάκτων στη Μακεδονία (1897); tirnavospress.gr 'Ο ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897 σε θεσσαλικό έδαφος'
note: Encircled by three Ottoman columns, the irregulars fought a last battle around Krania and dispersed; a late group under Sinsinikos heading for Nezeros was scattered too. All activity was over by 31 March/12 April.

name: Melouna
place: Melouna pass (Hasan Melouna – Melouna – Menexes), north of Tyrnavos
sources: el.wikipedia Μελούνα; stratistoria.wordpress.com 'Μάχη της Μελούνας (17–18 Απρ 1897)'; tr.wikipedia Osmanlı-Yunan Savaşı (1897) ('Milona geçidi'); tirnavospress.gr
note: Outpost fighting began on 17 April; the main Ottoman attack on 18 April drove the thin Greek line (3.5 companies on a 4 km front) back to Lygaria and Mati in disorder, opening Thessaly. Votanochori held until mid-afternoon; Tafil-Vrysi counter-attacked successfully before withdrawing.

date: 4–5 April 1897 O.S. (16–17 April N.S.); withdrawal 9–10 April O.S.
name: Nezeros
sources: en.wikipedia 1st Infantry Division (Greece) (1897 section); searchculture.gr (Μάχη στον κάτω Όλυμπο κοντά στο χωριό Νέζερο: evzones attacking Profitis Ilias hill); en.wikipedia Template:Campaignbox Greco-Turkish War (1897); en.wikipedia 1st Infantry Division (Greece): '[5 April] the Nezerou Detachment launched a major attack, captured most of the Turkish outposts', later forced back when the centre was 'overwhelmed by twenty-two Turkish battalions'; searchculture.gr photo record of the battle near Nezeros
borderline: A local Greek success on the right flank; the position was given up a few days later in the general retreat after Mati, so the result could also be read as indecisive.
note: After outpost skirmishing at Bairaktari on 4 April O.S., the Nezeros Detachment attacked on 5 April and took most of the Ottoman outposts on Lower Olympus (including the Profitis Ilias height), but the Greek centre was overwhelmed at Melouna–Mati and the detachment withdrew towards the Pineios on 9–10 April O.S.

name: Arta (1897)
place: Arta bridge, Imaret fort and the Arachthos crossings (Peranthi, Neochori, Pachykalamos)
sources: el.wikipedia Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897, Αμυντικός Στρατώνας Άρτας, Σαλαώρα; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897)
note: Artillery duel between the Arta barracks and the Ottoman Imaret fort and an Ottoman attack on the bridge, repulsed; next day Greek troops crossed by a pontoon bridge and took Neochori, Pachykalamos and Akropotamia after hard fighting; the Ottomans abandoned the Arta plain and Filippiada by 10/22 April.

name: Preveza (sea, 1897)
place: Strait of Preveza and the Ambracian Gulf (Salaora)
sources: el.wikipedia Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897, Σαλαώρα
borderline: ship-versus-fort bombardment rather than a fleet battle
note: The transport Makedonia was hit at the Preveza narrows and ran aground; Greek gunboats silenced Salaora's two Armstrong guns and Salaora was occupied on 10/22 April, but Preveza itself was not reduced. The Ottoman fleet stayed in the Dardanelles; the Eastern Squadron's bombardments of the Macedonian coast had no opposing force.

name: Reveni (Damasi)
place: Reveni pass near Damasi, west of Tyrnavos
sources: el.wikipedia Κωνσταντίνος Σμολένσκη, Δαμάσι Λάρισας; en.wikipedia Template:Campaignbox Greco-Turkish War (1897) ('Damasi')
note: Smolenskis held the passes he had fortified in 1885–86 for four days and the Ottomans withdrew without success; on 10 April (O.S.) GHQ ordered him to fall back with the rest of the army. en.wikipedia's campaign box calls the fighting in this sector 'Battle of Damasi' (probably the same action).

name: Mati
place: Mati, covering the road to Tyrnavos
sources: el.wikipedia Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897) ('outside the town of Tyrnavos'); tirnavospress.gr
note: Hard fighting on 21–22 April; on 23 April the Ottoman left advanced, the Greek staff ordered a withdrawal and the retreat turned into the panic of Tyrnavos and Larissa (Larissa occupied 27 April N.S.). Also called the battle of Tyrnavos.

name: Deleria
place: Deleria (Deliler) and Mousalar, Lousfaki–Deleria line, Larissa
sources: el.wikipedia Δελέρια Λάρισας; tirnavospress.gr 'Στα Δελέρια μάχη, στον Τύρναβο λεηλασία το 1897'; en.wikipedia Template:Campaignbox Greco-Turkish War (1897)
note: Deleria and Mousalar fell on the night of 11 April (O.S.), followed by the disorderly Greek retreat through Larissa to Farsala.

name: Pente Pigadia (1897)
sources: el.wikipedia Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897; en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897), Template:Campaignbox Greco-Turkish War (1897)
note: en.wikipedia says Manos captured Pente Pigadia on 23 April but the advance stalled for lack of reinforcements; el.wikipedia says Greek attacks on the fortified Ottoman position on 27–29 April achieved nothing. The Greek army then fell back towards Arta.

name: Velestino
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Velestino; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Βελεστίνου, Κωνσταντίνος Σμολένσκη
note: The only clear Greek victory of the Thessalian campaign; the Ottoman assaults of 29 and 30 April failed and Smolenskis became a national hero.

name: Velestino (second battle)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Velestino; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Βελεστίνου
note: The Greek left held on 5 May but was broken on 6 May; ordered to retire after Farsala, Smolenskis withdrew unmolested to Almyros. Volos fell on 8 May.

name: Farsala (1897)
place: Farsala (Drisklioi, Tatari, Teke heights, railway station)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη των Φαρσάλων (1897) (after Μεγάλη Στρατιωτική και Ναυτική Εγκυκλοπαίδεια); en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897)
note: The evzone outposts and the Philhellenic Legion fought a delaying action; by evening the Ottomans held the Enipeus crossings and the station and the Greeks withdrew in fair order overnight to Domokos. 'Italy' in allies_b stands for the Philhellene/Garibaldian volunteers, not the Italian state (volunteers serving in the Greek army count as Greece).

name: Nikopolis (1897)
sources: en.wikipedia Greco-Turkish War (1897); el.wikipedia Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897, Νικόπολη Πρέβεζας
note: The attempt to cut off Preveza failed with heavy Greek casualties.

name: Gribovo (1897)
sources: el.wikipedia Γρίμποβο Άρτας, Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897; en.wikipedia Template:Campaignbox Greco-Turkish War (1897)
note: The Greeks failed to take the ridge; with the right wing stopped, the whole second Epirus offensive was called off on 15 May. Not to be confused with the Battle of Gribovo of October 1912.

name: Strevina (Kryopigi)
sources: el.wikipedia Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897
note: The Greek centre attacked on the 13th and, reinforced from the left, took and held a defensive position on the 14th, but withdrew on 15 May after the failure at Gribovo.

name: Domokos
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Δομοκού, Ελληνοτουρκικός πόλεμος του 1897; en.wikipedia Battle of Domokos
note: The Garibaldian and Philhellenic volunteers (c. 3,000, mostly Italian) pinned the Ottoman right, but the Ottoman left turned the Greek right and the army withdrew that night to the Fourka pass. 'Italy' in allies_b stands for the Garibaldian volunteers, not the Italian state.

name: Ostima
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Όστιμας»; en.wikipedia Efthymios Kaoudis
note: About 20 Greeks under the Cretan Kaoudis against about 87 komitadjis; the Greeks took a hill and inflicted the losses until an Ottoman detachment intervened. Dates vary: 18 September (Kaoudis article) or 20–21 September 1904; one passage of the battle-sites page gives 1905.

name: Statista
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Στάτιστας – Θάνατος Παύλου Μελά»; en.wikipedia Pavlos Melas; army.gr; Dakin, The Greek Struggle in Macedonia
note: Melas and about 11 men, surrounded in two houses by an Ottoman detachment (allegedly tipped off by the IMRO chief Mitros Vlachos), fought until nightfall; Melas was mortally wounded during the breakout and most of his men escaped. The exact circumstances of his death are disputed. The village was renamed Melas.

name: Zelovo
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Ζελόβου»; D. Karamitsos, Μακεδονικός Αγώνας 1904-1908 (AUTh); istorikakastorias.blogspot.com, Ο Μακεδονικός Αγώνας μέρος 3ο
note: About 33–35 Greeks, with armed villagers of Pisoderi, against about 70 komitadjis; the Bulgarian dead are given as 12 (Karamitsos) or 24 (battle-sites project). Ended when Ottoman troops intervened; a Kastoria local history describes it as a failed encirclement from which the Bulgarians escaped. Dalipis's article dates it to 1905.

date: 10 March – November 1905 O.S. (23 March – November 1905 N.S.)
name: Theriso revolt
winner_first: Theriso rebels drew with Prince George's govt
sources: Brief (named as a civil case); general histories of the Cretan State (Holland & Markides; Kitromilides, Eleftherios Venizelos); not verified online this session
borderline: a revolt with scattered skirmishes between rebels, the Cretan Gendarmerie and the international troops, not one named battle; no individually named engagement could be verified (Greek Wikipedia blocked, English page rate-limited)
note: Rebels at Theriso demanded union with Greece; clashes with the gendarmerie and international detachments through spring and summer 1905. Ended in November 1905 with an amnesty and concessions; Prince George left Crete in 1906. 'Cretan rebels' is used here for 1905 (the brief lists it to 1898).

name: Zagoritsani
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Ζαγορίτσανης»; istorikakastorias.blogspot.com, Ο Μακεδονικός Αγώνας μέρος 3ο; D. Karamitsos, Μακεδονικός Αγώνας 1904-1908 (AUTh); en.wikipedia Greek Struggle for Macedonia
borderline: an attack by 160–200 andartes on a fortified Exarchist village; the armed defence was brief and most of the 60–79 dead were villagers, so it is often called a massacre
note: Greek accounts call it the battle of Zagoritsani; Bulgarian and many modern accounts the Zagorichani massacre. Armed komitadjis were among the dead and the village was burned.

name: Mouriki
place: Mouriki height, north-west of Vlasti, Kozani
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Μουρικίου»; istorikakastorias.blogspot.com, Ο Μακεδονικός Αγώνας μέρος 3ο
note: About 115 andartes against about 100 Ottoman troops, reinforced by about 200 from Vlasti; the Ottomans, hit from three sides in fog, retreated in disorder. Greek losses 3 killed and 3 wounded; Ottoman losses unknown. Afterwards about 3,000 troops hunted the bands, which largely dispersed.

name: Aetozi
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Αετοζίου»
note: A Greek ambush party set for an Exarchist band was betrayed and attacked by an Ottoman detachment from Sorovits (Amyntaio); Kalogerakis and three Cretans were killed.

name: Osnitsani
winner_first: Ottomans & Bulgarian bands beat Greek bands
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Οσνίτσανης»; D. Karamitsos, Μακεδονικός Αγώνας 1904-1908 (AUTh); en.wikipedia Stergios Goutas
note: About 85 andartes attacked about 100 komitadjis in the village; about 750 Ottoman troops intervened. Litsas and L. Petropoulakis were killed when their bomb exploded early; after about eight hours the Greeks retreated with about 24 dead (Karamitsos: 16), against 9 komitadjis and a claimed 140 or more Ottoman dead. Commemorated annually under Presidential Decree 759/1960. Site position approximate.

name: Gornitsovo
winner_first: Ottomans & Bulgarian bands beat Greek bands
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Γκορνιτσόβου»
note: A Greek attack on the Exarchist band of Tane in the village was betrayed (allegedly by the guide Sapountzis); waiting Ottoman troops surrounded the attackers and 12 andartes, including Nikoloudis, were killed.

name: Paleochori
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Παλαιοχωρίου»
note: About 60 andartes attacked about ten armed Exarchists barricaded in a stone house; Foufas and four others were killed and Zakas led the retreat to Vogatsiko. The village was renamed Foufas in 1932. Site position approximate.

name: Grentsi
winner_first: Greek bands beat Bulgarian bands & Ottomans
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Γκρέντσης»
note: Kersakov's komitadjis counter-attacked from the hills and withdrew after Kersakov was mortally wounded (19 komitadjis killed, 7 Greeks wounded); an Ottoman detachment then fought for about two hours before withdrawing. Captured villagers who tried to escape were shot.

name: Kalogeriko
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Καλογερικού»
note: About 150 Ottoman soldiers surrounded the band in the ravine; 23 andartes, including Germas and Tsimbidaros, were killed and 11 captured, and Zakas escaped wounded. Losnitsa was renamed Germas in 1928.

date: night of 12–13 May 1908 O.S. (25–26 May N.S.)
name: Kostenetsi
sources: Western Macedonian Battle Sites project (maxesditikismakedonias.gr), «Μάχη Κωστενετσίου»
borderline: attack on an Exarchist village with heavy loss of life and burning of houses
note: About 80 andartes surrounded and attacked the village from west and east; about 40 Exarchists were killed and 27 houses burned, for 2 Greek dead. Ottoman cavalry from Biglista (Albania) ended the fighting.

name: Typaldos revolt
place: Salamis Naval Base and the Salamis strait
sources: general histories of the 1909 Goudi period (e.g. Mavrogordatos; Papacosma, The Military in Greek Politics); not verified online this session
borderline: a naval mutiny with a short exchange of fire, not a battle in the usual sense; date not re-verified
note: Officers and sailors under Typaldos seized the Salamis arsenal and torpedo boats; loyal ships and shore artillery opened fire and the mutineers gave up after a short fight with a few killed. Mainly naval, with shore artillery.

name: Icaria revolt
sources: en.wikipedia Free State of Icaria; en.wikipedia Evangelos Koukoudeas; mytilene.gr (message of the North Aegean regional union president, 16 July 2021); en.wikipedia Free State of Icaria ('a battle on 17 July 1912' commemorated at Chrysostomos; Spanos 'the sole Ikarian killed in the fighting'; locals 'expelled the Turkish garrison'); mytilene.gr: 'μετά από διάφορες επικίνδυνες αψιμαχίες, είχαν αφοπλίσει και συλλάβει όλους τους Τούρκους του νησιού'
borderline: a revolt with only brief fighting against a small Ottoman gendarmerie garrison, not a named battle
note: On 17 July 1912 (O.S.) the islanders rose and, after several skirmishes in which one Icarian (Georgios Spanos of Evdilos) was killed at Chrysostomos, disarmed and captured the Ottoman garrison, which was shipped to Anatolia. The Free State of Icaria was declared on 18 July and joined Greece on 4 November 1912. 'Greek rebels' is used here for a 1912 revolt (the brief defines it before 1821).

name: Samos revolt
place: Samos; main fight at Bayraktari near Palaiokastro (east of Vathy)
sources: samosin.gr, The Unification of Samos with Greece; en.wikipedia Principality of Samos; en.wikipedia Pavlos Gyparis and Ioannis Karavitis; samosin.gr/?p=9827 (landing 7 September 1912; battle at Bayraktari, Paleokastro, 'lasted for a whole day, with many dead and wounded on both sides'; truce 13–18 September; 'on September 23, 1912 the Turkish army left Samos'); en.wikipedia Principality of Samos (garrison withdrew to Anatolia; enosis 11/24 November 1912)
borderline: The entry is the revolt as a whole; its one distinct named fight is Bayraktari (Palaiokastro).
note: Sofoulis landed at Ormos Marathokampou with armed Samians, Cretans and Icarians on 7/20 September 1912; the fiercest fight was a day-long battle at Bayraktari near Palaiokastro, where the Ottoman artillery stood, with many dead and wounded on both sides. After a truce brokered by the British consul (13–18 September O.S.), the garrison capitulated and left for Asia Minor on 23 September/6 October 1912. Union with Greece was declared on 11/24 November 1912; Greek troops landed on 2 March 1913.

name: Elassona
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913 (list of battles of the Macedonian front); Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913; en.wikipedia Battle of Yenidje (chronology)
note: Short opening battle on the first day of the Greek offensive; the Ottoman covering force fell back to Sarantaporo.

name: Gribovo
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pente Pigadia and Battle of Bizani (background); Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: The Army of Epirus crossed the Arta bridge and took the Gribovo heights (6 Oct O.S.); an Ottoman counter-attack (9 Oct) pushed it back towards Arta on the night of 10–11 Oct, but the Ottomans then withdrew and the Greeks took Filippiada unopposed on 12 Oct (O.S.). Greek accounts treat it as a repulse of the Ottoman attack.

name: Sarantaporo
place: Sarantaporo pass, between Elassona and Servia
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913; en.wikipedia Battle of Sarantaporo
note: First major Greek victory; opened the way to Servia and Kozani.

date: night of 31 October–1 November 1912 (18–19 Oct O.S.)
name: Thessaloniki harbour (Feth-i Bülend)
sources: en.wikipedia Ottoman ironclad Feth-i Bülend; en.wikipedia First Balkan War; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: Torpedo boat 11 slipped through the harbour defences and sank the ironclad Feth-i Bülend (used as a barracks/guard ship) with two torpedoes; 7 Ottoman dead, no Greek loss.

name: Yenidje
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913; en.wikipedia Battle of Yenidje; el.wikipedia Μάχη των Γιαννιτσών
note: Decisive battle that opened the road to Thessaloniki; related fighting at Burgas, the Balitzas bridge and Gida.

name: Nicopolis
sources: en.wikipedia First Balkan War and Preveza; en.wikipedia Battle of Pente Pigadia; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: Attack on the Preveza defences with the support of the Ionian squadron; Preveza surrendered on 21 Oct (O.S.).

name: Sorovich
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913 (listed as 'Σόροβιτς (Αμυνταίου), 23-24 Οκτ.'); Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913; en.wikipedia Battle of Sorovich
note: Greek 5th Division attacked at Banitsa/Zabardeni (21 Oct O.S.), held at Sorovich on 22–23 Oct, routed by a dawn attack on 24 Oct. The 'Battle of Vevi' in the en.wikipedia First Balkan War article is this action. ΓΕΣ dates it 23–24 Oct O.S.

name: Pente Pigadia
place: Pente Pigadia (Beshpinar), on the Preveza–Ioannina road
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913 (dated 24 Oct 1912 O.S.); en.wikipedia Battle of Pente Pigadia; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: Two Evzone battalions took and held the pass against repeated Ottoman counter-attacks; Ottomans withdrew to Pesta.

name: Metsovo
sources: en.wikipedia Metsovo; en.wikipedia Battle of Driskos (chronology)
note: Troops, Epirote bands and local volunteers crossed the Katara–Zygos ridge and attacked the garrison, which surrendered at 4 pm. en.wikipedia Driskos gives 27 Oct (O.S.) for the capture.

name: Himara
sources: en.wikipedia Himara Revolt; en.wikipedia List of Ottoman battles in the 20th century; el.wikipedia Εξέγερση της Χειμάρρας (1912)
note: Landing from Corfu and local rising expelled the Ottoman garrison; later Albanian attacks (Dec 1912) were repulsed. en.wikipedia First Balkan War and Battle of Bizani give 5 November without calendar; the Himara article gives 18 Nov N.S.

name: Lesbos
place: Mytilene to Filia and Klapados, Lesbos
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lesbos (1912); en.wikipedia List of Ottoman battles in the 20th century; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: Landing at Mytilene on 21 Nov (N.S.); the garrison withdrew to the fortified camp at Filia; the decisive fighting (Leimonas monastery, Filia–Klapados, 18–20 Dec N.S.) ended in the surrender of 21 Dec. Greek tradition calls the final action the battle of Klapados.

name: Chios
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Chios (1912); el.wikipedia Απελευθέρωση της Χίου; en.wikipedia List of Ottoman battles in the 20th century
note: Landing at Kontari; fighting for Karyes and the Aipos heights; final assault 2 Jan 1913 (N.S.) and surrender at Anavatos/Pityous on 3 Jan. 36 Greeks killed; c. 1,800 Ottomans captured.

name: Driskos
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Driskos; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Δρίσκου; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: The Garibaldini (mostly Greek volunteers with some Italians) and Cretan volunteers served within the Greek army, so count as Greece. The poet Lorentzos Mavilis was killed here.

name: Pesta
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913 (listed as 'Πεστών, 29 Νοεμ. 1912'); el.wikipedia Μάχη των Πεστών; ELISME, Η Μάχη των Πεστών (2022)
note: The Cretan student company of the Independent Cretan Regiment led the capture of Pesta; Ottomans fell back to the Bizani line.

date: 14–16 December 1912 (1–3 Dec O.S.); assault continued to 22 Dec
name: Manoliassa
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913 (listed as 'Μανωλιάσσας, 1-3 Δεκ. 1912'); en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani (first attack 14–22 Dec 1912)
note: First Greek attack on the Ioannina fortified zone; en.wikipedia says it was repulsed and the Ottomans gained some ground. Greek accounts treat Manoliassa as a battle in its own right and do not call it a defeat.

name: Elli
place: Off Cape Helles, mouth of the Dardanelles
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Elli; el.wikipedia Ναυμαχία της Έλλης; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: Averof's charge forced the Ottoman fleet back into the Straits. en.wikipedia gives 40°12′N 26°24′E, which lies inside the Straits; the action was fought just outside the entrance.

name: Korytsa
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Korytsa; el.wikipedia Κατάληψη της Κορυτσάς; en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani
note: Greek forces from western Macedonia drove Djavid Pasha's corps out of the Korçë area, cutting Ioannina's last supply route. en.wikipedia First Balkan War wrongly gives 20 November.

name: Lemnos (sea)
place: About 12 nautical miles south-east of Mudros, Lemnos
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lemnos (1913); Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: Last sortie of the Ottoman fleet; afterwards it stayed in the Dardanelles for the rest of the war.

name: Aetorrachi
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913 (listed as 'Αετοράχης, 7 Ιαν. 1913'); en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani (second attack, 20 Jan 1913)
note: Second Greek assault on the Bizani line: it gained ground and pushed the defenders back to the forts but was suspended after heavy losses and bad weather; Sapountzakis was then replaced.

name: Bizani
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913; en.wikipedia Battle of Bizani; el.wikipedia Απελευθέρωση των Ιωαννίνων
note: Final battle of the siege of Ioannina (Dec 1912–Mar 1913); the earlier assaults are entered as Manoliassa and Aetorrachi. Ioannina surrendered on the night of 6 March (21 Feb O.S.).

name: Angista (Pangaion)
place: Angitis river and Angista, Pangaion hills, Serres
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Angitis; en.wikipedia Second Balkan War (table of Greek–Bulgarian battles); EAAS, Ο Β΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος; en.wikipedia Battle of Angitis (23–24 May [O.S. 9–10 May] 1913, 'Bulgarian victory'; the Greeks were pushed back several km; Geshov ordered a halt on 10 May); EAAS, Ο Β΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος ('Την περίοδο από 10/23 έως 17/30 Μαΐου, στην περιοχή του Παγγαίου όρους η συμπλοκή εξελίχθηκε σε μάχη εκ του συστάδην', no result given)
borderline: Clash between nominal allies before the formal outbreak of the Second Balkan War.
note: Bulgarian accounts claim a victory, with the Greeks pushed back several km; Greek accounts describe close-quarter fighting on Pangaion on 23–30 May (10–17 May O.S.). Preceded by skirmishes in April–May at Paleochori, the Valchishta bridge and Levtera.

name: Thessaloniki (1913)
sources: EAAS, Ο Β΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος ('10ωρη μάχη', 1,259 prisoners); en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
borderline: Usually described as the disarming of the Bulgarian garrison rather than a named battle, although there was some ten hours of fighting.
note: The isolated Bulgarian battalion in the city was overrun after the Bulgarian surprise attack of 16 June (O.S.).

name: Kilkis–Lachanas
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία των Βαλκανικών Πολέμων 1912-1913; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913; en.wikipedia Battle of Kilkis–Lachanas; el.wikipedia Μάχη Κιλκίς-Λαχανά
note: Coordinates are Kilkis; the Lachanas wing (1st and 6th Divisions) fought about 30 km east (40.95, 23.25). Includes the recapture of Gevgelija and the Kalinovo hills (21 June O.S.); the 'Battle of Kalinovo' (Bulgarian victory) in the en.wikipedia Second Balkan War table is a sector of this battle.

name: Doiran
place: Doiran (Dojran), south-west shore of Lake Doiran
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Doiran (1913); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Δοϊράνης (1913); en.wikipedia Second Balkan War
note: Greek accounts sometimes date it 24–25 June (O.S.). Fighting ranged from the Doiran railway station (now Greece) to the town (now North Macedonia).

name: Vetrina (Demir Hisar)
place: Vetrina (Neo Petritsi) near Demir Hisar (Sidirokastro), Serres
sources: EAAS, Ο Β΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος ('διήμερη μάχη της Βετρίνας, ή Δεμίρ Ισάρ')
note: Two-day battle that opened the way to Serres and Sidirokastro; the Bulgarians burned Serres and Demir Hisar as they withdrew.

name: Kresna Gorge
place: Kresna gorge to Simitli and Gorna Dzhumaya, Struma valley
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kresna Gorge; en.wikipedia Second Balkan War; EAAS, Ο Β΄ Βαλκανικός Πόλεμος; Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913
note: The Greeks forced the gorge (completed 10/23 July) and took Simitli (26 July N.S.), then the Bulgarian counter-offensive threatened to encircle them: fighting at Hill 1378 near Gorna Dzhumaya (where Ioannis Velissariou fell on 13/26 July), the Predela pass (Predel Han) towards Razlog/Mehomia, and Pehčevo–Berovo. Ended by the armistice of 31 July (N.S.). Greek accounts stress the forcing of the gorge, Bulgarian ones the near-encirclement; en.wikipedia gives a stalemate.

name: Korçë (1914)
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus
note: Autonomists held part of the city for several days before gendarmerie reinforcements retook it on 27 March. Later (before the armistice of 7 May 1914) autonomist forces seized the Morava heights over Korçë.

name: Cepo monastery
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus
note: An Albanian gendarmerie push south into autonomist-held territory failed.

name: Berat (1914)
sources: en.wikipedia Autonomous Republic of Northern Epirus
note: An Epirote unit attacked the garrison and held the citadel for several days before withdrawing. el.wikipedia: "Κατάληψη του Βερατίου", 14 September 1914.

name: Thessaloniki (National Defence coup)
sources: en.wikipedia National Defence coup d'état; en.wikipedia Provisional Government of National Defence; el.wikipedia Κίνημα Εθνικής Αμύνης
note: About 600 Cretan gendarmes and volunteers blockaded III Corps HQ; a loyalist company tried to break out, 2 gendarmes killed and 3-4 soldiers hit before French officers stopped the shooting; loyalist troops were disarmed and shipped south. A standoff at the Mikro Karabournou artillery barracks the day before (29 Aug) ended without shooting.

name: Noemvriana (Athens)
sources: en.wikipedia Noemvriana; el.wikipedia Νοεμβριανά του 1916; Leon, Greece and the Great Powers 1914-1917
note: Royalist army (I Corps) and reservists (Epistratoi) against c. 2,500 French and British marines landed at Piraeus; Allied losses 191-227, royalist c. 82; the Allied squadron at Phaleron shelled parts of the city; the landing force withdrew under a compromise. Followed by royalist attacks on Venizelists in Athens (not a battle).

name: Nebyan cave (Otkaya)
place: Cave of the Virgin Mary near the monastery of Otkaya, Mount Nebyan (Nebiyan Dağı), Bafra–Samsun
sources: en.wikipedia Greek resistance during the Greek genocide; el.wikipedia Αντίσταση των Ποντίων στις αρχές του 20ού αιώνα
borderline: A siege that ended in collective suicide and massacre (Turkish sources: 'Meryemana Mağarası katliamı'); identification and date uncertain.
note: About 60 guerrillas defended 600–650 civilians for about a week against gendarmes, then an artillery-supported regiment; most civilians were killed after the defenders' suicide. Greek Wikipedia places a last stand of Pantel Amisou's band at Nebien Dağ in late 1917; probably the same event.

name: Skra-di-Legen
place: Skra (Liumnitsa) fortified position, north of Mt Paiko, Kilkis
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Skra-di-Legen; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Σκρα; en.wikipedia Archipelago Division; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Ο Ελληνικός Στρατός κατά τον Α΄ Παγκόσμιο Πόλεμο
note: Archipelago, Crete and Serres Divisions of the National Defence Corps with French support (British Empire also listed in the infobox). Greek losses c. 440 killed, c. 2,200 wounded, c. 160 missing; c. 2,000+ Bulgarians captured.

name: Dobro Pole
war: World War I (Macedonian front, Vardar offensive)
place: Dobro Pole, Zborsko and Sousnitsa heights, Kozhuf/Nidže range
winner_first: French, Serbs & Greeks beat Bulgarians & Germans
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dobro Pole; en.wikipedia Vardar offensive; en.wikipedia Archipelago Division
note: Greek Archipelago, 3rd and 4th Divisions (Gargalidis) on the French-Serbian flank: Franco-Greek regiments twice repulsed at Zborsko (c. 158 Greek dead), Greek units at Sousnitsa and on Mt Preslap (17 Sept), 6th Regiment took Zovik-Staravina-Cebren (18 Sept). Breakthrough that decided the Vardar offensive.

name: Doiran (1918)
war: World War I (Macedonian front, Vardar offensive)
place: Hills west of Lake Doiran (Pip Ridge, Grand Couronné) and between the lake and Belasica
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Doiran (1918); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Δοϊράνης (1918); en.wikipedia Vardar offensive; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ stelexi.army.gr Doirani dossier
note: Greek Serres and Crete Divisions (and the 14th Division on 19 Sept) with the British XII and XVI Corps; Greek losses 3,404-3,948. The Bulgarians repulsed all attacks but withdrew on 21 Sept after the Dobro Pole breakthrough.

name: Kherson (1919)
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Εκστρατεία στη Μεσημβρινή Ρωσία 1919 (dis.army.gr); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Χερσώνας; ru.wikipedia Украинский поход греческой армии; en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention
note: c. 700-850 Greeks (I/34th Regt, then two battalions of the 1st Regt) and c. 150 French plus some Volunteer Army troops against Grigoriev's brigade; Greek losses c. 257 (12 officers, 245 men); the Allies evacuated by sea on 10 March. Local Greek civilians were killed after the fall of the city.

name: Mykolaiv (1919)
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Εκστρατεία στη Μεσημβρινή Ρωσία 1919 ('occupation and abandonment of Nikolaev'); ru.wikipedia Украинский поход греческой армии; en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention
borderline: Mostly a negotiated evacuation; fighting limited to Grigoriev's failed attack of 7 March and skirmishes east of the city
note: c. 500 Greeks (7th Regiment) and two weak French companies, with an unreliable German garrison of c. 12,000; after the fall of Kherson the Allies withdrew by agreement on 14 March and Grigoriev entered the city, seizing large stocks of arms.

name: Berezivka
place: Berezivka (Berezovka) and Vasylynove, north-east of Odessa
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Εκστρατεία στη Μεσημβρινή Ρωσία 1919 ('Επιχειρήσεις Βασιλίνοβο και Μπερεζόφκα'); ru.wikipedia Украинский поход греческой армии; 'How Odessa became Red' (Battle of Berezovka, 18 March 1919)
note: A battalion of the Greek 34th Regiment with French zouaves, French Renault tanks and two Volunteer Army squadrons; attacks on 7 and 17 March were repulsed, but on 18 March an attack with armoured trains routed the French (who abandoned tanks and wounded); the Greeks fell back to Serbka. Greek losses 9 officers and 135 men.

name: Serbka–Buyalyk
place: Serbka station, Velykyi Buyalyk and Kapitanka line, north-east of Odessa
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Εκστρατεία στη Μεσημβρινή Ρωσία 1919 ('Επιχειρήσεις Σέρμπκα και Μπολ. Μπουγιαλίκ'); ru.wikipedia Украинский поход греческой армии; 'How Odessa became Red' (Cerbka retaken 27 March, turned 31 March)
note: Defence of the Odessa front: Kondylis's 3rd Regiment retook Serbka station and repulsed the general Red attack of 5 April; a Greek battalion at Pavlinka was nearly encircled; the line was abandoned when White units gave way and the Allies evacuated Odessa (3-7 April) without a final battle.

name: Sevastopol (1919)
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Εκστρατεία στη Μεσημβρινή Ρωσία 1919 ('Επιχειρήσεις στην Κριμαία', 24 March–28 April); ru.wikipedia Украинский поход греческой армии; en.wikipedia Southern Russia intervention
borderline: Greek role was the garrison (2nd Regiment, XIII Division) and naval gunfire; the repulse is credited mainly to French ships in English sources
note: The Red attack on the city was repulsed by fire from French and Russian ships and the Greek battleship Kilkis and destroyer Panthir; a truce followed on 17 April and the Allies evacuated by 28-29 April. Earlier fighting at the Perekop isthmus (Ishun) was by White units; a Greek company's clash with mutinous French sailors on 19 April was an incident, not a battle.

name: Smyrna landing
place: Smyrna (İzmir) harbour and the Sarı Kışla barracks
sources: en.wikipedia Greek landing at Smyrna; el.wikipedia Ελληνική απόβαση στη Σμύρνη; Llewellyn Smith, Ionian Vision, ch. 5
borderline: Largely unopposed Allied-sanctioned occupation; the fighting was a shooting incident at the barracks, not a pitched battle.
note: The Ottoman garrison had orders not to resist; after the first shot (attributed to Hasan Tahsin) Greek troops fired on the Sarı Kışla barracks and the garrison surrendered. Royal Navy and French warships were present. Turkish soldiers and civilians were killed in the aftermath.

name: Urla
sources: en.wikipedia Urla clashes; tr.wikipedia Urla Olayları
note: Turkish name Urla Olayları. The Turks were the local Ottoman garrison and a newly formed 120-man militia, counted as the first Kuva-yi Milliye unit. Greek troops landed from a warship and occupied Urla.

name: Ayvalık
sources: tr.wikipedia Ayvalık Cephesi; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
borderline: Local resistance to the occupation of Ayvalık; Turkish 'Ayvalık Cephesi' is more a front than a single battle.
note: Turkish name Ayvalık Cephesi. In Turkish tradition Ali Bey's men fired the first shots of armed resistance to the Greek occupation. The town was occupied by a Cretan detachment (8th Cretan Regiment) on 29 May.

name: Bergama (raid)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bergama; tr.wikipedia Bergama Baskını; ΔΙΣ, Επίτομος ιστορία της εις Μικράν Ασίαν εκστρατείας (1967); Μεγάλη Στρατιωτική και Ναυτική Εγκυκλοπαίδεια, 'Πέργαμος'
note: Turkish name Bergama Baskını. The first Greek defeat of the war: the newly arrived Greek garrison was surprised by Kuva-yi Milliye and regular troops, lost heavily and fell back to Menemen. English and Turkish Wikipedia treat the raid and the Greek recapture of 19–20 June as one event; they are split here because the outcomes differ.

name: Malgaç bridge raid
place: Malgaç railway bridge, 1–2 km east of Sultanhisar (Aydın–Nazilli railway)
sources: en.wikipedia Malgaç Raid; tr.wikipedia Malgaç Baskını
borderline: Small raid (about 60 attackers against a 20-man bridge guard).
note: Turkish name Malgaç Baskını. The bridge guard was wiped out and the bridge destroyed.

name: Bergama (recapture)
place: Heights SW and N of Bergama; Bakırçay bridge
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Bergama; tr.wikipedia Bergama Baskını; ΔΙΣ, Επίτομος ιστορία (1967)
note: Two Greek columns (6th Archipelago Regiment from Dikili and a detachment from Menemen) converged on the town; a Turkish rearguard covered the withdrawal to Soma and the Greeks entered Bergama on 20 June.

name: Erbeyli
place: Erbeyli railway station, between İncirliova and Aydın
sources: en.wikipedia Raid on Erbeyli; tr.wikipedia Erbeyli Baskını
borderline: Small raid.
note: Turkish name Erbeyli Baskını. A Kuva-yi Milliye raid on the station guard; the raiders withdrew when Greek reinforcements arrived (both wikis score it as a Greek victory, though Greek losses were about 30 killed). Civilians were massacred in reprisal.

name: Erikli
place: Erikli, west of Aydın near Erbeyli
sources: en.wikipedia Raid on Erikli; tr.wikipedia Erikli Baskını
borderline: Small raid.
note: Turkish name Erikli Baskını. Turkish account: Greek losses 30 killed and 40 wounded; the raiders returned to their positions afterwards.

name: Tellidede
place: Tellidede ridges (Ovaemir–Yeniköy–Kadıköy line), south of Aydın
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Tellidede; tr.wikipedia Tellidede muharebeleri
note: Turkish name Tellidede muharebeleri (dated 24–29 June there; English Wikipedia gives 25–26 June). The Turkish militia withdrew.

name: Aydın
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Aydın; tr.wikipedia Aydın Savunması; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
note: Turkish name Aydın Savunması ('Defence of Aydın'). Kuva-yi Milliye forces drove the Greeks out of the town on about 29–30 June; the 4th Infantry Regiment retook it on about 3–4 July. Much of the town burned and both Greek and Turkish civilians were massacred. Turkish accounts stress the temporary liberation.

name: Greek Summer Offensive (1920)
place: Western Anatolia: Akhisar, Soma, Salihli, Alaşehir (Philadelphia), Balıkesir, Bursa, Uşak
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Summer Offensive; tr.wikipedia 1920 Yunan Yaz Taarruzu; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας; Llewellyn Smith, Ionian Vision, ch. 8
borderline: A named offensive made up of many small actions rather than a single battle (listed as such in the campaign boxes).
note: Turkish name 1920 Yunan Yaz Taarruzu. Akhisar (22 June), Salihli and Soma (24 June), Alaşehir (25 June), Balıkesir (30 June), Bursa (8 July), Uşak (29 August). The Archipelago Division stormed fortified positions at Keresun near Soma on 29 June. British forces took Mudanya; Ottoman Kuva-yi Inzibatiye also fought the nationalists.

name: Eastern Thrace (1920)
place: Eastern Thrace: Evros crossing, Uzunköprü, Lüleburgaz, Adrianople; landings at Rodosto and Marmara Ereğlisi
sources: tr.wikipedia Trakya'nın İşgali; tr.wikipedia Türk Kurtuluş Savaşı kronolojisi
borderline: An offensive against limited resistance; no single named battle found in the sources consulted.
note: Turkish name Trakya'nın İşgali. Adrianople (Edirne) fell on 24–25 July 1920 and Cafer Tayyar was captured. Greek forces occupied Eastern Thrace until the Mudanya armistice (Oct 1922).

name: Gediz
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Gediz; tr.wikipedia Gediz Muharebeleri; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
note: Turkish name Gediz Muharebeleri. The Turks attacked on 24–25 October and entered Gediz on 26 October. The Greek 13th Division counter-attacked and re-entered it on 31 October, then evacuated Gediz on 12 November. English and Greek accounts score it as a Greek victory; Turkish accounts stress the first Greek withdrawal from occupied ground. The irregulars' poor showing led Ankara to build a regular army.

name: Servetiye front (Izmit)
sources: tr.wikipedia Servetiye Cephesi; tr.wikipedia İzmit'in işgali
borderline: A front of skirmishes lasting months rather than a single battle; poorly sourced article.
note: Turkish names Servetiye Cephesi and İzmit'in işgali. Kuva-yi Milliye and the Kocaeli Group harassed the Greek garrison. Greek troops evacuated Bahçecik on 27 June and Izmit on 28 June 1921, partly as a planned redeployment before the July offensive. The Izmit massacres accompanied the withdrawal.

name: First İnönü
sources: en.wikipedia First Battle of İnönü; tr.wikipedia Birinci İnönü Muharebesi; el.wikipedia Πρώτη μάχη του Ινονού
note: Turkish name Birinci İnönü Muharebesi. Greek sources call it an 'offensive reconnaissance' (επιθετική αναγνώριση) towards Eskişehir, broken off by design, so Greek losses were small; the Turks claim a victory, the first of the new regular army.

name: Second İnönü
place: İnönü and Kovalıca (Kovalitsa), west of Eskişehir
sources: en.wikipedia Second Battle of İnönü; tr.wikipedia İkinci İnönü Muharebesi; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
note: Turkish name İkinci İnönü Muharebesi. The Greek III Corps took the Kovalitsa position but failed to break through at Metristepe and fell back to Bursa.

name: Afyonkarahisar (March 1921)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αφιόν Καραχισάρ; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
note: The southern arm of the March offensive. Greek Wikipedia's dates are Old Style (14–16 March). The I Corps took Dumlupınar and then Afyon, then evacuated the city on 6 April after the failure at İnönü.

date: 8–15 April 1921 (Aslıhanlar 8 April, then Turkish attacks on the Dumlupınar line)
name: Aslıhanlar–Dumlupınar (1921)
place: Aslıhanlar and the Dumlupınar (Tulu Punar) position
sources: tr.wikipedia Refet Bele; tr.wikipedia İkinci İnönü Muharebesi; sozcu.com.tr '100 yılında İnönü savaşları' (Aslıhanlar 8 April 1921; Greeks evacuated Afyon and withdrew to Dumlupınar); TÜBA history series ch. 6, footnote citing the Turkish General Staff volume 'Aslıhanlar ve Dumlupınar Muharebeleri (9 Kasım 1920 – 15 Nisan 1921)'; en.wikipedia Second Battle of İnönü
borderline: No dedicated article; the day of the main Dumlupınar attack is not confirmed. Turkish General Staff volume title: 'Aslıhanlar ve Dumlupınar Muharebeleri (9 Kasım 1920 – 15 Nisan 1921)'.
note: Turkish names Aslıhanlar and Dumlupınar Muharebeleri. After the Greek III Corps' retreat from İnönü, the I Corps gave up Afyon and fell back to the Dumlupınar line, fighting at Aslıhanlar on 8 April; Refet's attacks on Dumlupınar then failed to dislodge it. Turkish sources call the result inconclusive (Afyon was regained), but Mustafa Kemal treated it as a defeat: Refet was relieved and the fronts were merged under İsmet.

name: Afyonkarahisar (July 1921)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
note: Opening action of the Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir (tr: Kütahya-Eskişehir Muharebeleri, 10–24 July 1921). Greek historiography lists Afyon, Kütahya and Eskişehir as separate battles; they are given separately here.

name: Kütahya (1921)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Κιουτάχειας; en.wikipedia Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir; el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας
note: Greek Wikipedia's date is Old Style (2–4 July). The Turkish army escaped the planned encirclement and fell back on Eskişehir; the 10th Division entered Kütahya on 17 July. Part of the Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir.

name: Eskişehir (1921)
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Εσκί Σεχίρ; en.wikipedia Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir; tr.wikipedia Kütahya-Eskişehir Muharebeleri
note: Greek Wikipedia's date is Old Style (8–9 July). The III Corps took Eskişehir and İsmet's counter-attack of 20–21 July was repulsed; the Turkish army withdrew east of the Sakarya. This is the decisive phase of the Battle of Kütahya–Eskişehir (Turkish: Kütahya-Eskişehir Muharebeleri).

name: Sakarya
place: East of the Sakarya river, Polatlı–Haymana (Kale Grotto, Çal Dağ, Duatepe)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Sakarya; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Σαγγαρίου; tr.wikipedia Sakarya Meydan Muharebesi; Llewellyn Smith, Ionian Vision, ch. 11
note: Turkish name Sakarya Meydan Muharebesi ('Officers' Battle'). Includes the actions at Kale Grotto, Mangal Dağ, Çal Dağ (taken by the Greeks on 2 Sept) and Duatepe. Greek Wikipedia calls the outcome indecisive, but the Greek army withdrew west of the Sakarya (ordered 10 Sept), a Turkish strategic victory.

name: Santa (1921)
place: Santa (Dumanlı) villages and the Magara cave, Gümüşhane
sources: el.wikipedia Σάντα (Τουρκία); en.wikipedia Greek resistance during the Greek genocide; el.wikipedia Αντίσταση των Ποντίων στις αρχές του 20ού αιώνα
borderline: Partisan sources; sequence of events unclear.
note: Greek Wikipedia says the Santa guerrillas resisted the Turkish attack of 6 Sept 1921 successfully. English Wikipedia says the Kemalists occupied Santa, but Kourtidis' band beat off the attack on the Magara cave and escaped with about 300 women and children. Scored as a draw. An earlier Greek success at Kopalanta (Κοπαλάντων) is mentioned without a date.

name: Topçam (first battle)
sources: el.wikipedia Κοτζά Αναστάς; el.wikipedia Αντίσταση των Ποντίων στις αρχές του 20ού αιώνα
borderline: Partisan Greek sources only; a prolonged siege or sweep rather than a single action.
note: A Turkish division under Liva Pasha attacked the guerrilla refuge, sheltering some 12,000 civilians, for 52 days without taking it. Greek sources give 700 Turkish soldiers killed.

name: Topçam–Dazli (second Topçam battle)
place: Dazli and the Topçam mountains, SW of Erbaa
sources: el.wikipedia Κοτζά Αναστάς; en.wikipedia Seventh Battle of Dazli (background); el.wikipedia Αντίσταση των Ποντίων στις αρχές του 20ού αιώνα
borderline: Partisan sources; dates and identification uncertain.
note: Greek accounts: Cemal Cevit's 'Operation Yıldırım', with about 10,000 men, was routed on 23 Feb 1922 and he was killed. Turkish records cited in English Wikipedia describe a four-day clash at Dazli from 18 January 1922. Probably one or more of the six earlier Dazli battles.

name: Dazli (seventh battle)
place: Dazli, about 28 km SW of Erbaa (Dazlı Deresi), Pontus
sources: en.wikipedia Seventh Battle of Dazli (Aslanidis, Ποντιακή Εστία 1950; TBMM Zabıt Ceridesi)
note: A night counter-attack by about 60 guerrillas, with a relief force of about 200, routed the besieging force (said to number 10,000 regulars and irregulars). The Turks carried off and massacred more than 200 Greek women and children. A Grand National Assembly record mentions the clash at 'Dazlı Deresi'.

name: Afyonkarahisar–Kocatepe (1922)
place: Greek lines SW of Afyonkarahisar (Tınaztepe, Kalecik Sivrisi, Erkmentepe), directed from Kocatepe
sources: tr.wikipedia Büyük Taarruz; tr.wikipedia Başkomutanlık Meydan Muharebesi; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αλή Βεράν; en.wikipedia Great Offensive
note: Opening of the Great Offensive (Büyük Taarruz): the Turks broke through the Greek 4th and 1st Divisions' lines after a heavy bombardment, Plastiras' counter-attack on 27 Aug failed, and Afyon was evacuated. English Wikipedia's 'Battle of Dumlupınar' (26–30 Aug) covers this entry and the next two.

name: Toumlou Bounar (Frangou group)
place: Dumlupınar (Toumlou Bounar) defensive position; Tuklu Tepe
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αλή Βεράν (section 'Η Μάχη στο Τουμλού-Μπουνάρ'); ΔΙΣ, Επίτομος ιστορία (1967)
note: Greek Wikipedia's date is Old Style (16 Aug). The Turks took Tuklu Tepe, splitting the Greek army into the Frangou and Trikoupis groups. Frangou withdrew west towards Uşak, covered by Plastiras' 5/42 Evzone Regiment.

name: Dumlupınar (Ali Veran)
place: Ali Veran valley and Ada hills, between the Akar river and Dumlupınar (Zafertepe/Çal area)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Dumlupınar; tr.wikipedia Başkomutanlık Meydan Muharebesi; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αλή Βεράν; Llewellyn Smith, Ionian Vision, ch. 12
note: Turkish name Başkomutanlık Meydan Muharebesi ('Battle of the Commander-in-Chief'), celebrated on 30 August. Greek Wikipedia's date is Old Style (17 Aug). The encircled Trikoupis group was shattered: it lost its artillery, transport and wounded and broke out westward at night. Greek accounts note that the remaining units held the field until dark.

name: Uşak (Trikoupis group)
place: Murat Dağ – Karaja Hisar, NE of Uşak
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αλή Βεράν (section 'Μετά την μάχη'); tr.wikipedia Başkomutanlık Meydan Muharebesi; tr.wikipedia Büyük Taarruz
borderline: Mainly a fighting retreat that ended in surrender, rather than a distinct battle.
note: After a five-day march under constant attack, Trikoupis and Digenis surrendered at Karaja Hisar on 2 Sept (Old Style 20 Aug) with about 190 officers and 4,400 men. Turkish sources give 6,000 men and place the surrender at Uşak, calling it the last action of the Başkomutanlık battle. Trikoupis learned there that he had been named commander-in-chief. A column under Gen. Dimaras surrendered on the Murat Dağ.

name: Salihli (1922)
sources: el.wikipedia Χρονολόγιο στρατιωτικών επιχειρήσεων Μικρασιατικής εκστρατείας; ΔΙΣ, Επίτομος ιστορία (1967); sabah.com.tr (Erdal Şafak, 'Ege'de Eylül': Salihli among towns taken on 5 September 1922); Greek and Turkish searches found no account of the fighting itself
borderline: Rearguard action known mainly from Greek accounts; no dedicated article.
note: Greek units repulsed a Turkish attack at Salihli, keeping the road open for the retreat to the embarkation ports, then withdrew. Turkish chronology records Salihli liberated on 5 Sept. Scored as a Greek tactical success.

name: Leonardopoulos–Gargalidis coup (Macedonia)
place: Central and western Macedonia (government forces from Thessaloniki against Ziras's rebel units)
sources: en.wikipedia Leonardopoulos–Gargalidis coup attempt; el.wikipedia Κίνημα Λεοναρδόπουλου-Γαργαλίδη
note: Government forces regained northern Greece by 25 October and Ziras fled to Yugoslavia. In the Peloponnese, Leonardopoulos and Gargalidis crossed the Isthmus toward Athens, were surrounded and surrendered unconditionally on 27 October without a recorded battle.

date: 22–28 October 1925 (border clash at Demir Kapia 18–19 October)
name: Petrich incident
war: Incident at Petrich (War of the Stray Dog)
place: Belasitsa border (Demir Kapia pass) and the approaches to Petrich
sources: en.wikipedia Incident at Petrich; el.wikipedia Επεισόδιο του Πετριτσίου; en.wikipedia Second Hellenic Republic
note: After a Greek soldier/outpost was shot at Demir Kapia, c. 20,000 Greek troops entered Bulgaria (22 Oct) against border guards, IMRO chetas and local volunteers; the League of Nations ceasefire came hours before the planned assault on Petrich, which Greek accounts and some newspapers reported taken and Bulgarian accounts say held. Greece withdrew and paid £45,000 (a Bulgarian diplomatic victory). c. 50 Bulgarian dead (mostly civilians); Greek dead put at 121 by Bulgarian estimate.

name: Athens (Republican Guard, 1926)
place: Athens, barracks of the Republican Guard
sources: en.wikipedia Napoleon Zervas; The National Herald, 'From Dictatorship to Democracy in Greece, 1926' (9 September); Venizelos Foundation archive (trial of Zervas and Dertilis, September 1926); The National Herald (1926 retrospective); en.wikipedia Napoleon Zervas; searchculture.gr Venizelos archive
borderline: Exact barracks/site within Athens not identified (loc approx)
note: Kondylis, who had overthrown Pangalos on 22 August 1926, ordered the Republican Guard disbanded; on 9 September its battalions under Lt-Cols Zervas and Dertilis resisted and were overpowered in Athens by government troops reinforced from Chalcis. Contemporary press gives about 70 killed and 130 wounded, many of them in the street unrest that followed. Zervas and Dertilis were court-martialled and sentenced to life imprisonment (amnestied 1928).

name: Athens (1935 coup)
place: Athens: Military Academy (Evelpidon) and Makrygianni barracks
sources: en.wikipedia Greek coup attempt of 1935; Veremis, Η Ελλάδα του Μεσοπολέμου (cited there)
note: On the night of 1 March rebel officers seized units in Athens (Evelpidon academy, Makrygianni barracks) while the fleet at Salamis mutinied; government troops retook them by 2 March and the capital stayed in government hands.

name: Strymon (1935)
place: Strymon river crossing (Kalfa bridge) west of Serres
sources: en.wikipedia 1935 Greek coup attempt ('quickly suppressed the Movement in Macedonia after a series of conflicts'; Kammenos fled to Bulgaria on 11 March); contemporary press summarised at globalsecurity.org 'Cretan Uprising of 1935' (government troops took Serres as the rebels withdrew east); protothema.gr (Kammenos's IV Corps, c. 8,000 men, on the Strymon with a second line on the Nestos); en.wikipedia 1935 Greek coup attempt; globalsecurity.org Cretan Uprising of 1935; protothema.gr article on the coup of 1 March 1935
borderline: Kalfa-bridge site and exact day of the fighting not confirmed online; the decisive government advance and the rebel collapse on 11 March are confirmed
note: Kondylis's forces from Thessaloniki, with air support, forced the Strymon line held by Kammenos's IV Corps (Serres-Drama-Kavala); the rebel front collapsed and Kammenos fled to Bulgaria on 11 March. Government aircraft also reportedly bombed rebel-held Serres and Drama.

name: Pindus
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pindus; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Πίνδου; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία του Ελληνοϊταλικού και Ελληνογερμανικού Πολέμου 1940–1941
note: The Julia Division took Vovousa (2 November) but was surrounded and driven back with heavy loss; Davakis was gravely wounded on 2 November. Frontier cleared by 13 November.

date: 2–8 November 1940 (Italian offensive in Epirus from 28 October)
name: Elaia–Kalamas
place: Kalpaki (Elaia) and the Kalamas river line, Ioannina–Thesprotia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Elaia–Kalamas; el.wikipedia Μάχη Ελαίας - Καλαμά; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία 1940–1941
note: Also called the Battle of Kalpaki. Igoumenitsa fell on 6 November, but the Italian offensive was halted on 8 November and the Greeks were back on the whole Kalamas line by 13 November.

name: Morava–Ivan
place: Morava and Ivan mountains, south-east of Korçë
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Morava–Ivan; el.wikipedia Μάχη Μόροβα-Ιβάν; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Επίτομη Ιστορία 1940–1941
note: Opening battle of the Greek counter-offensive; the breach of the Morava–Ivan line led to the fall of Korçë on 22 November.

name: Pogradec
place: Pogradec and its surroundings, Lake Ohrid
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pogradec; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Πόγραδετς
note: Some sources give 1 December for the fall of the town, and 24–25 November for the start of operations.

name: Saranda
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Saranda; el.wikipedia Μάχη των Αγίων Σαράντα
note: Port taken on 6 December 1940; nearby Delvinë fell in the same days (folded in here). en.wikipedia names Cavallero as the Italian commander, but he only took over on 29 December.

name: Himara
place: Himarë and Mount Pilur (Mali i Xhorët), Albanian coast
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Himara; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Χειμάρρας
note: Porto Palermo taken on 13 December; Evzone bayonet charge on Mount Pilur on 19 December; Himara entered on 22 December.

name: Papanikolis convoy attack
place: Off Sazan island, approaches to Vlorë
sources: en.wikipedia Greek submarine Papanikolis (Y-2); Hellenic Navy history
borderline: A submarine attack on Italian shipping rather than a battle; known in Greek naval histories by the boat's name.
note: en.wikipedia credits the motor ship Antonietta (22 December) and the troop transport Firenze (23 December, near Sazan); which ships were sunk differs between Greek and Italian records.

name: Proteus convoy attack
sources: Hellenic Navy history (submarine Proteus Y-3); not verified online in this batch
borderline: An attack by a submarine on a convoy, not a battle named in standard lists; details from memory, not checked against a source in this batch.
note: Proteus torpedoed and sank the transport Sardegna (c. 11,450 GRT) in an escorted convoy and was then rammed and sunk with all hands by the torpedo boat Antares. Scored as a draw: each side lost a ship.

name: Klisura Pass
sources: en.wikipedia Capture of Klisura Pass; el.wikipedia Κατάληψη της Κλεισούρας
note: Italian counter-attacks failed and the 'Lupi di Toscana' Division was nearly destroyed. Not the same place as the Kleisoura Pass in Kastoria (April 1941).

name: Trebeshinë
place: Mount Trebeshinë (Height 1923), between Këlcyrë and Tepelenë
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Trebeshina; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Τρεμπεσίνας
note: The Greeks took and held the Trebeshinë massif but did not reach Tepelenë; the 5th (Cretan) Division lost 5,776 men and was no longer fit to fight. The February attempts towards Tepelenë are folded in here.

name: Hill 731
place: Hill 731, at the foot of Mount Trebeshinë, north of Këlcyrë
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Hill 731; el.wikipedia Μάχη στο Ύψωμα 731
note: Part of the Italian Spring Offensive; the hill held through at least 18 assaults.

name: Popotlivitsa
sources: el.wikipedia Οχυρό Ποποτλίβιτσα; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Αγών κατά της γερμανικής εισβολής
note: Western end of the line. Held until the surrender of 10 April; the fort-level outcome comes from Greek accounts and was not checked against a fort-by-fort source.

name: Istibei
place: Fort Istibei, Beles range west of Rupel
sources: el.wikipedia Οχυρό Ιστίμπεη; en.wikipedia Fort Istimpei; Greek GHQ communiqué no. 164 (via Mertzos, EMS 2016); ww2wrecks.com
note: Fell on 7 April after heavy fighting.

name: Kelkayia
place: Fort Kelkayia (Spani Petra), Beles range west of Rupel
sources: Greek GHQ communiqué no. 164 (via Mertzos, EMS 2016); ΓΕΣ (army.gr), Η μάχη των οχυρών
note: Fell on 7 April along with Istibei.

name: Arpaluki
place: Fort Arpaluki (Stirigma), Beles range west of Rupel
sources: ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Αγών κατά της γερμανικής εισβολής; ww2wrecks.com (Arpalouki complex)
note: Greek accounts say it held until the surrender of 10 April; this was not checked against a fort-by-fort source.

name: Paliouriones
place: Fort Paliouriones, west of the Rupel gorge
sources: Mertzos, Τα οχυρά (EMS 2016, with German eyewitness accounts); ΓΕΣ (army.gr), Η μάχη των οχυρών
note: Beat off strong attacks on 7 April; the last fort to surrender, on 10 April. The checklist's 'Paliouriotes' is this fort.

name: Rupel
place: Fort Rupel and the Usita outwork, Rupel gorge of the Strymon
sources: en.wikipedia Fort Roupel; el.wikipedia Ρούπελ; ΓΕΣ (army.gr), Η μάχη των οχυρών; Mertzos (EMS 2016)
note: Not taken: the German attack was stopped here 6–9 April. The garrison left with honours only after the East Macedonia Army Section capitulated on 9/10 April.

name: Perithori
place: Fort Perithori, east of Rupel (Agkistro sector)
sources: Mertzos, Τα οχυρά (EMS 2016); ΓΕΣ (army.gr), Η μάχη των οχυρών
note: On 9 April the fort commander refused his division's order to surrender and held out all day; the surrender followed on 10 April.

name: Lisse
place: Fort Lisse (with neighbouring Dasavli), Nevrokopi plateau, Drama
sources: en.wikipedia Fort Lisse; el.wikipedia Οχυρό Λίσσε; vrellis.gr
note: Held against repeated attacks; the Dasavli–Lisse front is credited with heavy German losses for very few Greek casualties. It is not verified that the 72nd Division was the attacker here.

name: Echinos
place: Fort Echinos, Rhodope north of Xanthi
sources: Greek GHQ communiqué no. 164 (via Mertzos, EMS 2016); ΓΕΣ (army.gr), Η μάχη των οχυρών
note: Reported still holding on 7 April and blocking heavy equipment; it surrendered with the rest under the capitulation.

name: Nymfaia
sources: el.wikipedia Οχυρό Νυμφαίας; Greek GHQ communiqué no. 164 (via Mertzos, EMS 2016)
note: Reported holding against attacks on 7 April; the same communiqué says the Western Thrace forces were withdrawn in good order, so its role is ambiguous.

name: Vevi
place: Klidi pass and Kelli, near Vevi, Florina
winner_first: Germans beat Australians, British, New Zealanders & Greeks
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Vevi (1941); en.wikipedia Battle of Greece
note: Also called the Battle of the Klidi Pass. Greek units: the Dodecanese Regiment and the X Border Sector at Kelli, and the I/88 Battalion at Radosi.

name: Kleisoura Pass (1941)
place: Kleisoura pass between Mt Vitsi and Mt Siniatsiko, Kastoria
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kleisoura Pass; el.wikipedia Μάχη της στενωπού της Κλεισούρας
note: The 80th Regiment was destroyed, but its stand delayed the German advance by almost a day. Not the same place as the Klisura Pass in Albania (January 1941).

name: Maleme
place: Maleme airfield and Hill 107, west of Chania
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Maleme
borderline: The Greek part was small: gendarmes and armed Cretan villagers, with no Greek regiment at the airfield.
note: Losing Hill 107 and the airfield let the Germans fly in reinforcements, which decided the battle for Crete.

name: Kastelli Kissamou
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Crete; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Μάχη της Κρήτης
note: The 1st Greek Regiment, with gendarmes, cadets and armed civilians, wiped out the Mürbe paratroop detachment on 20 May. German forces took Kastelli on 24 May, and Greek remnants fought on nearby until about 26 May. Scored on the 20 May action.

name: Galatas
place: Galatas heights and Prison Valley, south-west of Chania
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Crete; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Μάχη της Κρήτης
borderline: Greek role (6th Greek Regiment and armed civilians under the 10th NZ Brigade) was not verified online for this entry.
note: Galatas fell on 25 May, was retaken briefly in a New Zealand night counter-attack, and was then abandoned.

name: Alikianos
place: Alikianos, head of Prison Valley, south-west of Chania
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Crete; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ, Η Μάχη της Κρήτης
note: The 8th Regiment and local volunteers held off the engineers and two parachute battalions, charging with the bayonet when ammunition ran out. A combined air and mountain-troop attack broke through on 27 May. Greek accounts treat it as a successful stand that bought at least 24 hours for the retreat to Sfakia.

name: Heraklion
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Heraklion; en.wikipedia Battle of Crete
note: On 20 May the Greek 3rd and 7th Regiments and the Garrison Battalion, with civilians, retook the western barracks, town gates and docks. The garrison held until the British evacuation on the night of 28/29 May. en.wikipedia scores it a German victory, though many accounts call it an Allied tactical success.

name: Rethymno
place: Rethymno airstrip (Pigi–Stavromenos), Hill A and the town
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Rethymno
note: Greek units: the 4th and 5th Regiments and about 800 Gendarmerie cadets. The defenders held the airfield and town until German columns arrived from Chania, and Campbell surrendered on 29/30 May.

name: Kandanos
place: Kandanos and the Floria pass, Selino, south-west Crete
sources: el.wikipedia Ολοκαύτωμα της Κανδάνου; en.wikipedia Battle of Crete
borderline: Fought mainly by armed Cretan civilians (with some soldiers and gendarmes) rather than an army unit; the dates were not verified online.
note: Local irregulars ambushed the German column heading for Paleochora. The punitive destruction of the village on 3 June 1941 is not part of this entry.

name: Drama uprising
place: Drama, Doxato, Choristi, Prosotsani and other villages of the Drama district
sources: en.wikipedia Drama uprising; en.wikipedia Greek Resistance; in.gr, 28η Οκτωβρίου, ημέρα μνήμης για την Εθνική Αντίσταση; Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece
note: Insurgents organized by the local KKE attacked Bulgarian gendarmerie posts and officials in Drama, Doxato, Choristi and nearby villages. Rebels killed six or seven Bulgarian policemen at Doxato and briefly declared a people's government at Prosotsani; most leaders were killed by 29 September. In reprisal the Bulgarians executed 485 men at Doxato and Choristi on 29 September and some 360–500 in Drama (Bulgarian reports: up to 1,600 Greek dead in all; Greek sources: thousands). Grouped under 'Greek resistance (other)' because ELAS did not yet exist (EAM was founded on 27 September 1941).

name: Reka
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη της Ρεκάς
note: The first armed clash between ELAS and Italian troops in occupied Greece; ELAS won.

name: El Alamein (second battle)
place: El Alamein line, Western Desert (Greek brigade in the southern sector under 50th Division)
sources: en.wikipedia Second Battle of El Alamein (Greece in belligerents); en.wikipedia Greek Armed Forces in the Middle East; en.wikipedia Pafsanias Katsotas
note: The 1st Greek Infantry Brigade (about 4,500 men) fought under the British 50th (Northumbrian) Division, XIII Corps, in the southern half of the line, and stayed in the following operations until 19 December 1942. Greek losses: 89 killed (6 officers, 83 men), 228 wounded. Coordinates are those of the battle, not the exact Greek sector. Some works end the battle on 11 November.

name: Leivadi
place: Livadi (Leivadi) and its surroundings, Elassona district, Larissa
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Leivadi (Μάχη του Λιβαδιού)
note: About 500 guerrillas and armed villagers drove the Italian garrison troops back to Elassona and took 17 prisoners. The military results were small, but Italian requisitioning raids in the area stopped.

name: Triton (off Kafireas)
sources: USNI Proceedings, 'The Greek Navy Fights On' (Aug. 1944); laststandonzombieisland.com, HS Triton
borderline: single-submarine action against convoy escorts; not usually styled a battle
note: Triton attacked a German convoy (one supply ship reported sunk or damaged) and was then hunted for some six hours by the subchaser UJ-2102 and the destroyer ZG3 Hermes (the ex-Greek Vasilefs Georgios). She fought on the surface after being disabled and was rammed and sunk by UJ-2102. About 20 crew and two Allied liaison officers were killed and some 17 captured.

name: Gorgopotamos
place: Gorgopotamos railway viaduct, south of Lamia, Phthiotis
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Resistance; en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army; Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece; Myers, Greek Entanglement
note: ELAS and EDES guerrillas overwhelmed the Italian guard posts at both ends of the bridge while British sappers blew up two spans, cutting the Thessaloniki–Athens railway for weeks. The only joint ELAS–EDES operation.

name: Uarsciek (sinking of)
sources: en.wikipedia Italian submarine Uarsciek; en.wikipedia Greek destroyer Vasilissa Olga; uboat.net, Royal Hellenic Navy
borderline: ship-versus-submarine action rather than a named battle
note: Uarsciek fired torpedoes at a cruiser force and was depth-charged to the surface by HMS Petard and the Greek destroyer Vasilissa Olga, then hit by their gunfire as she tried to fight with her deck gun. Her captain and 17 men were killed. She was boarded but sank under tow. Some sources say 14/15 December.

name: Mikro Chorio
sources: in.gr, 28η Οκτωβρίου, ημέρα μνήμης για την Εθνική Αντίσταση (μάχη του Μικρού Χωριού); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (18/12/42)
note: ELAS guerrillas defeated an Italian column sent into Evrytania after Gorgopotamos. The exact day differs between accounts.

name: Meritsa (Oxyneia)
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη της Μερίτσας
note: About 800 ELAS fighters.

name: Fardykambos
place: Fardykambos, Vigla pass and Aliakmon bridge, between Siatista and Grevena
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Fardykambos; en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army; ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1943; greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές
note: An ambush of an Italian supply convoy grew into a 52-hour battle in which about 2,000 guerrillas, reserve officers and villagers surrounded the relief column from Grevena. The Italians lost 96 dead and about 550–565 prisoners; Grevena was evacuated soon after. PAO members took part as individuals (Kontonasios took general command).

name: Ksar Ghilane
place: Ksar Ghilane (Ksar Rhilane) oasis, southern Tunisia
sources: army.gr, Ιστορία του Ιερού Λόχου (ΓΕΣ); en.wikipedia Sacred Squadron (Greece); lki.gr, The Sacred Squadron; cheminsdememoire.gouv.fr, La colonne Leclerc
note: First battle of the Sacred Squadron (Ieros Lochos). The Franco-Greek Force L, dug in at the oasis, beat off an Axis mechanised column with RAF support, covering the flank march around the Mareth Line. The French account names elements of the German 90th Light Africa Division. Three men of the Sacred Squadron were missing. RAF air support is folded in.

name: Mareth Line
place: Mareth Line and Tebaga Gap, southern Tunisia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Mareth Line (Greece in belligerents; order of battle lists Leclerc Force with the Greek Sacred Squadron under the New Zealand Corps); lki.gr, The Sacred Squadron
borderline: Greek role was flank protection with Leclerc's Force L; one action on 19 March 1943 with 1 killed, 1 wounded
note: The Sacred Squadron served with Leclerc's Force L on the left flank of the New Zealand Corps' outflanking march through the Tebaga Gap. The Greek official history records no separate named action here apart from Ksar Ghilane (10 March).

name: Wadi Akarit
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Wadi Akarit (Greece in belligerents); army.gr, Ιστορία του Ιερού Λόχου; en.wikipedia Sacred Squadron (Greece)
note: A mixed Greek–New Zealand detachment (the Sacred Squadron was attached to the 2nd New Zealand Division from 29 March) fought on 6 April. Cavalry Capt. G. Bourdakos was killed. The Wikipedia order of battle also lists a '1st Greek Infantry Brigade' with the 50th Division, but that brigade had returned to Egypt in December 1942, so the listing seems to be an error.

name: 5/42 Regiment (first dissolution)
sources: en.wikipedia National and Social Liberation (chronology); Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece
borderline: Forced dissolution of a resistance unit; the extent of fighting and the sites are not given in the sources consulted.
note: ELAS attacked the 5/42 Regiment on 14 May and again on 23 June 1943, forcing its dissolution; it was re-formed in July under the National Bands Agreement after British pressure.

name: Messina Convoy
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of the Messina Convoy (outcome 'inconclusive'); en.wikipedia Greek destroyer Vasilissa Olga; uboat.net Vasilissa Olga
note: HMS Jervis and the Greek destroyer Vasilissa Olga sank the lone escort, the torpedo boat Castore, but the two merchant ships (Vragnizza, Postumia) were only damaged and reached Messina. At the time the Allies claimed the whole convoy, and Greek accounts often repeat that claim.

name: Porta
sources: en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army (battle of Porta, many Italians killed); ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1943; greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (8–9/6/43)
note: ELAS units of Thessaly fought an Italian force at the Porta pass where the Pindus meets the Thessalian plain. The chronicles date it 8–9 June 1943; ELAS's list of important battles places it in summer 1943.

name: Sarantaporo (1943)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Sarantaporos (1943); en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army (battle of Sarantaporo, 99 Germans killed)
note: ELAS ambush, with charges laid under British SOE direction, of a German supply column of the 117th Jäger Division in the Sarantaporo pass on the first day of Operation Animals: of about 108 Germans, 24 were killed and 79 captured (most executed on 13 July) and all vehicles destroyed; ELAS sources give 99 Germans killed. Not to be confused with the 1912 battle of Sarantaporo.

name: Myrtia (Gouritsa)
