sources: en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army (battle of Myrtia, July 1943); ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1943 (7–10 July 1943, Gouritsa); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (10/7/43, Gouritsa, against Germans)
note: Fighting between ELAS of Aetolia-Acarnania and German troops moving into western Greece in July 1943. Outcome set to draw because the sources consulted give none.

name: Sicily (Allied invasion)
place: Sicily (Greek ships off the east coast: Augusta, Catania)
winner_first: US, British & Greeks beat Italians & Germans
sources: en.wikipedia Allied invasion of Sicily (Kingdom of Greece in belligerents; Kanaris led the attack on Augusta); naval-history.net HMS Bolebroke (Pindos), HMS Modbury (Miaoulis); uboat.net Kanaris, Vasilissa Olga; USNI Proceedings 1944
borderline: Greek role was naval (escort, cover and fire support), not a ground unit
note: Greek destroyers Kanaris, Miaoulis, Pindos, Adrias and Vasilissa Olga took part. On 12 July Kanaris was the first Allied ship into Augusta harbour, under shore-battery fire, and supported the commando landing. Vasilissa Olga bombarded Catania. Greek sources claim that on 20–21 July Adrias and HMS Quantock fought three German E-boats and sank one or two, but this is unconfirmed. The main arm of the campaign was the land fighting.

name: Leontio
sources: ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1943 (16-hour battle against III Battalion, 'Piemonte' Division); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (14/7/43)
note: ELAS of Achaea fought an Italian battalion of the Piemonte Division for about 16 hours; ELAS sources say the Italian force was destroyed.

name: Makrynoros (1943)
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Μακρυνόρους
note: Part of Operation Animals; EDES ambushed and beat the Brennero division's column.

name: Trahili
place: Trahili, above Vorizia, southern slopes of Psiloritis, Heraklion
sources: en.wikipedia Vorizia (Battle of Trahili, 15 August 1943); en.wikipedia Greek Resistance
note: Petrakogiorgis' band, heavily outnumbered, fought a German force all day and escaped; the partisans lost 7 men and the Germans 13. In reprisal the Germans razed Vorizia on 27 August 1943 (excluded). Recorded as a draw (the guerrillas held out and withdrew).

name: U-458 (sinking of)
sources: uboat.net U-458 (sunk by HMS Easton and the Greek Pindos); uboat.net Fighting the U-boats: Greece; naval-history.net HMS Bolebroke
borderline: ship-versus-submarine action rather than a named battle
note: U-458 was depth-charged by Easton and Pindos and rammed by Easton. 8 of the crew died and 39 were captured. This is the only U-boat kill that uboat.net credits to the Royal Hellenic Navy. (U-407, sunk south of Milos on 19 September 1944, was sunk by British and Polish ships, not Greek ones.)

name: ELAS–PAO conflict (1943)
place: Kilkis area, Nigrita and Chalkidiki, central Macedonia
sources: en.wikipedia Panhellenic Liberation Organization; Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War
borderline: A campaign of clashes rather than one named battle.
note: ELAS pressed PAO bands in the Kilkis area to disarm and then destroyed PAO's armed units in a small civil war lasting until December 1943; PAO remnants later served in German-directed anti-communist units.

name: Salerno
sources: naval-history.net HMS Bolebroke (Pindos 'present at the landings, providing inshore gunfire support and AA defence'); en.wikipedia Operation Avalanche (Greece not listed)
borderline: Greek role was a single escort destroyer (Pindos) giving gunfire support and anti-aircraft defence; Greece is not listed among the belligerents in standard accounts
note: Vasilissa Olga also escorted convoys for Avalanche. The battle's main arm was the land fighting for the beachhead.

name: Arachova (1943)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army (battle of Arachova, September 1943); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (10–11/9/43; German attack 27/10/43)
note: At the Italian armistice ELAS attacked an Italian convoy and disarmed an Italian battalion at Arachova and fought a German column; ELAS sources say the Germans were repelled on 10 September but forced ELAS to withdraw on 11 September. The Germans attacked Arachova again on 27 October 1943. Not the 1826 battle of Arachova.

name: Kato Symi
sources: en.wikipedia Viannos massacres; Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece
note: After Bandouvas' men killed the two soldiers of the German post at Kato Symi (10 September), a German infantry company sent to investigate was ambushed by about 40 guerrillas on 12 September and defeated with heavy losses; 12 Germans were captured. The Germans answered with the Viannos massacres (14–16 September 1943), which are not part of this entry.

name: Katsonis (off Skiathos)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek submarine Katsonis (Y-1); en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign (casualty table); sa-snd.gr, Η συμβολή του ΠΝ στα Δωδεκάνησα
borderline: single-submarine action; not usually styled a battle
note: While trying to attack a German troop transport, Katsonis was depth-charged to the surface. She fought the subchaser UJ-2101 (the ex-Greek minesweeper Strymon) with her deck gun until she was rammed and sunk. 32 men were killed, including Laskos, 15 were captured and 3 swam to Skiathos. This is Laskos' well-known 'last fight'.

name: Stampalia convoy action
sources: en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign; en.wikipedia Greek destroyer Vasilissa Olga; sa-snd.gr, Η συμβολή του ΠΝ στα Δωδεκάνησα
borderline: convoy interception without a standard battle name (descriptive name)
note: Faulknor, Eclipse and Vasilissa Olga sank the German transports Pluto and Paula. Their escort UJ-2104 was forced to beach. The Greek Navy history dates the action 21–22 September and estimates 700–900 German dead. Wikipedia gives 17/18 September.

name: Leros
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Leros (Greece listed as naval support; Greek losses 1 destroyer, 68 killed); en.wikipedia Dodecanese campaign; naval-history.net HMS Modbury (Miaoulis); sa-snd.gr, Η συμβολή του ΠΝ στα Δωδεκάνησα
note: Wikipedia dates the battle from the first Luftwaffe attacks to the surrender. The German landings were on 12–16 November. Greek role (naval): on 26 September Ju 88s sank Vasilissa Olga in Lakki harbour, killing 70–72 including her captain, Blessas. Miaoulis rescued the crew of HMS Panther (9 October). On 17 October Miaoulis and HMS Hursley shot up shipping in Kalymnos and sank UJ-2109. Adrias lost her bow to a mine off Kalymnos (22 October). Pindos bombarded German troops on Leros (12 November). Italy here is the co-belligerent Kingdom of Italy, fighting on the Allied side.

name: Dervenochoria (Pyli)
place: Pyli and the Dervenochoria villages, Boeotia
sources: greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (15–16/10/43, Pyli Dervenochorion); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα (two German companies trapped at Kerpini and in the Dervenochoria); ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1943
note: Fought at the same time as Kerpini; ELAS-aligned sources say German companies were trapped and destroyed in both places (over 150 German dead in all). el.wikipedia (17 October 1943): after an initial success it ended in an ELAS defeat.

name: Kerpini
place: Kerpini and Rogoi, near Kalavryta, Achaea
sources: Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece; en.wikipedia Massacre of Kalavryta (78 prisoners); ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1943 (16–17 October 1943, Goula–Mylioi, Rogoi); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές; greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα
note: ELAS surrounded a German company of the 117th Jäger Division; after the fighting 78 Germans were prisoners (ELAS chronicle: 19 dead, 65 captured on 16–17 October). The prisoners were shot in December during the German Operation Kalavryta, which ended in the Kalavryta massacre of 13 December 1943 (excluded).

name: ELAS–EDES conflict (1943–44)
place: Valtos, Tzoumerka and the Arachthos valley, Epirus and Aetolia-Acarnania
sources: Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece; Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; en.wikipedia Greek Resistance (Epirus ELAS–EDES conflict, October 1943 – February 1944); en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army
borderline: A campaign (the 'first round' of the civil war) rather than one named battle.
note: ELAS attacked EDES and drove it out of much of its territory in October–November 1943, while also breaking up smaller groups elsewhere; Zervas counter-attacked across the Arachthos in January 1944 and recovered most of his ground. The fighting ended in the Plaka armistice under British mediation. German operations hit both sides at the same time.

name: Kokkinia (1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kokkinia; en.wikipedia Greek Resistance; ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1944-1945 ('η θρυλική μάχη της Κοκκινιάς')
note: ELAS and EPON, with the residents, fought off four days of attacks by the Wehrmacht, the collaborationist Gendarmerie and Security Battalions; the Germans withdrew taking 300 residents, 50 of whom were shot at Chaidari on 9 March. Distinct from the Kokkinia blockade and executions of 17 August 1944 (a massacre, excluded).

name: Kaisariani (1944)
place: Kaisariani, Zografou and neighbouring quarters, Athens
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Resistance (Battle of Kaisariani, April 1944); en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army; ethniki-antistasi-dse.gr, Χρονικό του ένοπλου αγώνα 1944-1945
note: ELAS of Athens and local residents repelled attacks of Security Battalions, police and German troops on the 'red' eastern quarters. The executions at the Kaisariani firing range on 1 May 1944 are not part of this entry.

name: Klima (5/42 Regiment)
place: Klima (Efpalio) and the surrounding area, Doris, Phocis
sources: en.wikipedia National and Social Liberation (attack of 14 April 1944; the regiment held out three days); en.wikipedia Dimitrios Psarros (died at Klima Efpaliou, 17 April 1944); en.wikipedia Greek People's Liberation Army; Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece; Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; en.wikipedia National and Social Liberation; en.wikipedia Dimitrios Psarros; en.wikipedia Efpalio (Klima is a community of the Efpalio unit)
note: ELAS attacked the 5/42 Evzone Regiment of EKKA on 14 April 1944; the regiment held out for three days and then broke up near the coast of Doris; some men crossed the Corinthian Gulf, but most were captured with Colonel Psarros, who died at Klima on 17 April (Easter Monday), and executed. Whether Psarros was killed in the fighting or in captivity is disputed.

name: Alexandria naval mutiny (suppression)
name_el: Κίνημα της Μέσης Ανατολής (κατάληψη των πλοίων)
war: Second World War (Greek mutiny in the Middle East)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Armed Forces in the Middle East ('Eleven seamen were killed, others wounded'); en.wikipedia Petros Voulgaris (appointed 21 April, oversaw 'the violent recapture of the mutinied ships')
borderline: suppression of a mutiny, not a named battle
note: Officer detachments loyal to the government stormed and retook the mutinous ships. 11 seamen were killed and others wounded. The exact night (22/23 April) is not firmly confirmed. The army side of the mutiny (the 1st and 2nd Brigades, from 6 April) was ended when British troops surrounded the brigades and they surrendered. No Greek-on-Greek battle there was found, so it is folded in here.

name: Achladokampos khan
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο χάνι Αχλαδοκάμπου (1944)
note: An ambush on a convoy that destroyed the German unit.

name: Nikolitsi
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη στο Νικολίτσι

name: Normandy landings
place: Normandy coast (Greek corvette Kriezis with Force G, Gold Beach)
sources: en.wikipedia Normandy landings (Greece in belligerents); Kalogerakis, Η ελληνική συμβολή στην απόβαση της Νορμανδίας (elisme.gr, 2024)
borderline: Greek role was convoy escort by two corvettes (Kriezis, Tompazis) that came under German air attack; they did not fight enemy ships
note: Kriezis escorted the 50th Division assault convoy from the Solent to Normandy on 5–6 June and came under air attack on the return passage. Afterwards she led 12 cross-Channel convoys. Tompazis escorted convoys on 14–18 June. Seven Greek merchant ships took part, four of them scuttled as blockships. Greek air squadrons were in Italy, not Normandy.

name: Steiri
sources: Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece; en.wikipedia Distomo massacre (partisan attack on the convoy, 10 June 1944); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα
note: ELAS attacked an SS-Polizei column returning from an anti-partisan sweep near Steiri; the Germans fought their way out and then committed the Distomo massacre the same day, which is excluded. Recorded as a draw.

name: Valtetsi (1944)
sources: el.wikipedia: Μάχη του Βαλτετσίου (1944)
note: ELAS against the Valtetsi security company raised from the villagers.

name: Paramythia (1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Expulsion of Cham Albanians (18 June 1944); en.wikipedia National Republican Greek League (chronology: Paramythia and Parga liberated 29 June)
note: EDES, with Allied support, attacked the combined German–Cham garrison and took the town after a short fight; killings of Cham civilians in Paramythia and nearby villages followed (27 June). The EDES chronology dates the liberation of Paramythia and Parga to 29 June. Later German and Cham attempts to retake the town failed.

name: Stymfalia (1944)
sources: greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα (German combat detachment decimated); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (German clearing in Corinthia, battles at Psari and Stymfalia)
note: Fought during a German clearing operation in Corinthia in early July 1944.

name: Northern Pindus (Operation Steinadler)
place: Northern Pindus and Grevena, western Macedonia–Epirus
sources: greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (3/7/44: German clearing operation in northern Pindus, fifteen days; 22/7/44 Grevena retaken); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα (Operation 'Chrysaetos', July 1944)
borderline: A named German anti-partisan operation rather than a named battle.
note: The Germans swept the ELAS base area of the northern Pindus for about two weeks; ELAS units evaded and fought, and retook Grevena after the Germans withdrew (22 July). Recorded as a draw.

name: Amfilochia (1944)
sources: greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα (12–13 July 1944); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (13/7/44)
note: About 200 ELAS fighters attacked and held off infantry and tanks in the open for ten hours, withdrawing when a third of them had been killed or wounded.

name: Symi (raid)
sources: en.wikipedia Raid on Symi (Operation Tenement); army.gr, Ιστορία του Ιερού Λόχου; lki.gr, The Sacred Squadron
note: About 224 men of the Sacred Squadron and about 100 of the SBS overwhelmed the German garrison (with Italian carabinieri). 21 were killed and 151 captured, and an E-boat, 2 barges and 19 caïques were destroyed before the force withdrew as planned. Wikipedia gives Allied losses as 8 wounded and 2 drowned, while the Greek accounts give 9 Greek and 3 British killed.

name: Chora (1944)
sources: greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα (117th Jäger Division convoy, 99 dead and missing); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (19/7/44)
note: ELAS ambushed a truck convoy of the 117th Jäger Division north-west of Pylos; the Germans recorded 99 dead and missing.

name: Damasta
sources: en.wikipedia Damasta sabotage; en.wikipedia Greek Resistance
note: The group ambushed a German force (a truck of infantry and an armoured car) heading for Anogeia at the Damastos bridge; 35 Germans and 10 Italians were killed and 12 taken prisoner. The Germans answered with the destruction of Anogeia (13 August 1944) and executions at Damasta (excluded).

name: Menina
sources: en.wikipedia Expulsion of Cham Albanians (Battle of Menina, 17–18 August 1944); en.wikipedia National Republican Greek League (Menina 30 June; Fort Menina 17–18 August)
note: EDES defeated a German–Cham force and took Fort Menina during its July–August offensive in Thesprotia; afterwards the Cham community crossed into Albania en masse, and the Cham leaders Nuri and Mazar Dino left with the Germans. The EDES chronology also records a victory at Menina on 30 June 1944.

name: Karoutes
sources: greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, 1944: Μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ στην υπόδουλη Ελλάδα (Karoutes, August 1944); greekcivilwar.wordpress.com, Οι μάχες του ΕΛΑΣ με τους κατακτητές (5/8/44, Karoutes, Giona)
note: ELAS trapped a column of an SS mountain regiment; ELAS accounts claim about 200 Germans killed.

name: Kalamata (1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Meligalas (background) and Battle of Kalamata (1944); Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece
note: The Germans left Kalamata on 5 September; after the prefect Perrotis refused to disarm, ELAS attacked at dawn on 9 September and took the town. Survivors fled to Meligalas. On 17 September a crowd in Kalamata lynched prisoners, including Perrotis (excluded).

name: Pyrgos (1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Meligalas (background: ELAS attacked Pyrgos on 9 September and took it on 10 September); Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War
note: After a standoff with the local battalion commander, ELAS attacked the Security Battalion garrison of Pyrgos on 9 September and took the town on 10 September.

name: Rimini
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Rimini (1944) (Greece in belligerents); en.wikipedia 3rd Greek Mountain Brigade; army.gr, Occupation of Rimini by the III Greek Mountain Brigade; flamesofwar.com, 3rd Greek Mountain Brigade
note: The 3rd Greek Mountain Brigade fought under I Canadian Corps with New Zealand tank support. Before the battle it held off German attacks near Cattolica on 8 and 10 September. It took Monaldini and Monticelli on 13–14 September, losing almost 100 men, fought for Rimini airfield on 15–17 September and entered Rimini on 21 September. The mayor surrendered the city to the brigade, which earned the title 'Rimini Brigade' (Ταξιαρχία Ρίμινι). Part of the Gothic Line offensive (Operation Olive).

name: Meligalas
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Meligalas; Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece
note: About 1,200 ELAS fighters broke the defences of about 1,000 Security Battalion men after three days; ELAS lost over 150 dead. Hundreds of prisoners and civilians (estimates 700–1,100) were then executed, many at the Pigada well; the executions are not part of the battle.

name: Tripoli (1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Meligalas (background: Tripoli held out under siege until late September)
borderline: Siege; extent of fighting not stated in the sources consulted.
note: Tripoli was the last large Security Battalion stronghold in the Peloponnese; Papadongonas held out against the ELAS siege until late September and then surrendered to a British unit. Recorded as a draw.

name: Kilkis (1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Kilkis (battle of 4 November 1944); Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; Mazower, Inside Hitler's Greece
note: After the German withdrawal ELAS defeated the Security Battalions of Macedonia and armed nationalist bands (Michalagas and others) that had gathered at Kilkis; many prisoners were executed afterwards.

name: Thiseio
sources: en.wikipedia Dekemvriana and Organization X (ELAS attack on X, 4 December 1944); en.wikipedia Georgios Grivas (X fought at the Theseion); Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War
borderline: Named by place in Greek accounts; may be treated as part of the opening ELAS attacks rather than a separate battle. The outcome follows Greek accounts and was not verified online.
note: ELAS reservists besieged Grivas' Organization X in its Thiseio stronghold; British troops intervened and the X men were taken out under British protection. Organization X is grouped under 'Greek resistance (other)'.

name: Makrygianni
place: Gendarmerie barracks at Makrygianni, below the Acropolis, Athens
sources: en.wikipedia Makrygianni ('a violent battle took place there during the Dekemvriana'); Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece
note: ELAS repeatedly attacked the Gendarmerie barracks at Makrygianni; the gendarmes held out until British forces relieved them. Commemorated on the Right as the 'defence of Makrygianni'.

name: Kifisia (RAF headquarters)
sources: en.wikipedia Kifisia; Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece; Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War
note: ELAS besieged and captured the RAF headquarters in the hotels of Kefalari, Kifisia; the en.wikipedia Kifisia article dates the attack and surrender to the night of 16–17 December. Several hundred RAF personnel were taken prisoner and marched north, and released at Trikala after the truce. A British-only opponent, but marked civil as part of the Dekemvriana, as the brief requires.

name: Epirus (ELAS against EDES, 1944)
name_el: Επίθεση του ΕΛΑΣ κατά του ΕΔΕΣ (Δεκέμβριος 1944)
sources: en.wikipedia Dekemvriana (Epirus clashes); en.wikipedia Aris Velouchiotis; en.wikipedia National Republican Greek League; Woodhouse, The Apple of Discord / The Struggle for Greece; Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War
borderline: A short campaign rather than one named battle.
note: During the Dekemvriana ELAS attacked and broke up EDES in Epirus within about a week; Zervas and the remnants of his forces were evacuated by British ships from Preveza to Corfu.

name: Litochoro
sources: en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece; el.wikipedia Ελληνικός εμφύλιος πόλεμος
borderline: a raid on a gendarmerie post
note: About 33 guerrillas struck the station on the eve of the elections, killing 13 gendarmes; conventionally the start of the Civil War.

name: Deskati
sources: el.wikipedia Προσωρινή Δημοκρατική Κυβέρνηση; searches in Greek and English found no account (en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece, Greek Civil War and Provisional Democratic Government do not mention Deskati)
borderline: temporary capture of a town; details not checked
note: The guerrillas held Deskati briefly.

name: Skra (1946)
sources: el.wikipedia Ελληνικός εμφύλιος πόλεμος
note: Over 300 guerrillas attacked an army company at Skra and took the village.

name: Metsovo (1947)
sources: metsovomuseum.gr (Metsovo, 18–24 October and 3–6 November 1947: 'The Democratic Army of Greece fails to occupy Metsovo'); Close, The Origins of the Greek Civil War; ΓΕΣ/ΔΙΣ
note: DSE attacks on Metsovo on 18–24 October and again on 3–6 November 1947 failed to take the town.

name: Konitsa
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Konitsa; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Κόνιτσας
note: The DSE tried to take Konitsa as the seat of its Provisional Government; about 1,200 DSE fighters were killed.

name: Operation Limnes
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Limnes
borderline: a DSE plan and its defeat rather than a single battle
note: The DSE plan to take Thessaloniki for a "Free Greece" in Macedonia and Thrace; a National Army victory.

name: Kalavryta (1948)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Kalavryta
note: The DSE took the town from its government garrison.

name: Operation Dawn (Haravgi)
sources: el.wikipedia Παλαιοβράχα Φθιώτιδας; Α΄ Μοίρα Καταδρομών
borderline: a clearing operation
note: The National Army's clearing of Roumeli; the DSE lost men but most escaped.

name: Grammos (Operation Koronis)
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Koronis; Democratic Army of Greece
note: One of the largest battles of the war; a tactical National Army victory, but the DSE slipped away to Vitsi.

name: Vitsi (1948)
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Koronis (8,000 DSE fighters withdrew to Vitsi); FRUS 1948 vol. IV doc. 129 (telegram of 26 October 1948: third phase of the Vitsi operation from 15 October 'generally speaking a failure', the 'Vitsi setback'); en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece; history.state.gov FRUS 1948 vol. IV doc. 129; en.wikipedia Operation Koronis
borderline: start date approximate (after the end of Grammos on 20–21 August 1948)
note: The National Army's attacks on the DSE's Vitsi stronghold after Grammos failed in successive phases, the last from 15 October 1948; US officials called it the 'Vitsi setback'.

name: Karditsa
sources: en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece
note: The DSE took Karditsa briefly.

name: Operation Peristera
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Peristera
borderline: a campaign rather than a single battle
note: The clearing of the Peloponnese.

name: Naousa (1949)
sources: en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece; el.wikipedia Νάουσα
note: The DSE held the town for three days; an earlier raid had been made in December 1948.

date: 20/21 January – c. 9 February 1949 (town held for 19 days)
name: Karpenisi (1949)
sources: alfavita.gr, 'Μικρό σημείωμα για τον καπετάν Διαμάντη' (Karpenisi taken in January 1949 by the 2nd and 1st Divisions and held for 19 days); en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece; alfavita.gr article on kapetan Diamantis; en.wikipedia Democratic Army of Greece
note: The DSE took Karpenisi and held it for 19 days before withdrawing in early February.

name: Agios Vasileios
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Agios Vasileios
note: Part of Operation Peristera.

name: Florina (1949)
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Florina (1949); el.wikipedia Μάχη της Φλώρινας
note: The DSE's attempt to take Florina failed with heavy losses.

name: Operation Pyravlos
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Pyravlos
borderline: a campaign rather than a single battle
note: The defeat of the DSE in Central Greece.

name: Metaxades
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Metaxades
note: The DSE's last attempt to operate outside its fortified areas.

name: Vitsi (Operation Pyrsos)
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Pyrsos
note: The second phase of Operation Pyrsos broke the DSE on Vitsi.

name: Grammos (Operation Pyrsos)
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Pyrsos
note: The last battle of the Civil War; the DSE's remnants crossed into Albania.

name: Hill 381
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); Korean MND Institute for Military History, 이천 381고지 전투 (via ko wiki 그리스 한국 원정군); protothema.gr, Κορέα, Ύψωμα 381 (2025); in.gr (2025)
note: Part of Operation Thunderbolt; the Greek battalion served as 4th Battalion of the US 7th Cavalry. Three night attacks repulsed, ended about 04:30 on 30 January. Greek losses 11 killed, 14 wounded, 1 missing (Korean official history; Greek press: 9 killed, 14 wounded); Chinese losses claimed at 650–800. Some Greek articles misplace it near 'Incheon': it is Icheon.

name: Hill 326
place: Hills 325–326, east of Yongdu-ri, Yangpyeong, Gyeonggi
winner_first: Greeks & US v Chinese, result unknown
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); in.gr and eurohoops.net Greek summaries (Υψώματα 325 και 326, March 1951); en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea) ('March 7: Attack on Hill 326, east of Yongdu-ri'); en.wikipedia Operation Ripper (IX Corps advanced against light to moderate resistance and reached the Albany Line by 12 March); thekwe.org (Greek dead on 7 March 1951); in.gr, mfa.gr, koreanmedals.com
borderline: result not found; one of the five main battles in el.wikipedia's list
note: Opening day of Operation Ripper. Greek sources call it the battle of Hills 325 and 326; result not stated in the sources consulted. Site identification approximate.

name: Scotch Hill (Hill 313)
place: Hill 313 ('Scotch'), north of Yeoncheon, near the Imjin
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); Korean MND Institute for Military History, 연천 313고지 전투; in.gr (2025); thekwe.org Greek participation (US Presidential Unit Citation)
note: Part of Operation Commando. Attacks on 3 and 4 October repulsed (14 killed each day); hill taken about 14:00 on 5 October. The Greeks' costliest battle in Korea: 28 killed, about 85 wounded (105 casualties in all). Earned a US Presidential Unit Citation.

name: Nori Hill
place: Big Nori hill, Imjin double horseshoe bend, Yeoncheon
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); Hellenic War Museum (warmuseum.gr) on Tamvakas; thekwe.org (Bekiaris Silver Star citation); in.gr (2025)
note: The Greek 2nd Company took Big Nori and repulsed two counterattacks; Bekiaris was killed preparing for a third. en.wikipedia also lists a Greek attack on 'Big Nori Hill' on 26 September 1951, probably a duplicate of this action.

name: Outpost Harry
place: Outpost Harry (Hill 420), east of the Cheorwon valley, Iron Triangle
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); en.wikipedia Outpost Harry; army.gr (2024); Korean MND Institute for Military History, 철원 420고지 전투; military.com (2025)
note: The Greek battalion took over the outpost on 16 June and beat off the attack of the PVA 221st Regiment on the night of 17–18 June (Greek losses 5 killed, 20 wounded per the Korean official history). Greek Company P shared a US Distinguished Unit Citation. The Greeks called it 'Haros'. army.gr names Lt Col Arbouzis as commander, but he had left in 1951.

name: Hill 495
place: Hill 495, south of Bukjeongnyeong, southwest of Kumsong (Gimhwa area)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); Korean MND Institute for Military History, 북정령 전투 (Battle of Bukjeongnyeong, 16–26 July 1953)
note: During the Chinese Kumsong offensive. Hand-to-hand fighting on the half-fortified hill; the position held. The Korean official history groups this and Hill 492 as one Battle of Bukjeongnyeong (Greek losses 19 killed, 28 wounded overall). Site may lie in or near today's DMZ.

name: Hill 492
place: Hills 492 and 532, south of Bukjeongnyeong, near the Seungam pass (Gimhwa area)
sources: en.wikipedia Greek Expeditionary Force (Korea); Greek Embassy in Seoul, list of battles of the Sparta Battalion (mfa.gr, 2023); Korean MND Institute for Military History, 북정령 전투
note: The battalion held Hills 492, 532 and the 595 ridge; attacks on 21, 23 and 24 July and the final assault of 25–26 July (the last battle before the armistice of 27 July) were repulsed; 105 Chinese killed and 27 captured claimed. Part of the Battle of Bukjeongnyeong in Korean sources.

name: Spilia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Spilia; el.wikipedia Μάχη στα Σπήλια; eoka.org.cy, Σύντομη Ιστορική Αναφορά; Digenis Foundation EOKA calendar
note: About 12 guerrillas broke out of a cordon of some 700 British troops (Royal Marines, Parachute Regiment, Gordon Highlanders), who fired on each other in fog. Greek Cypriot accounts claim 15 British killed and 35 wounded; British losses are disputed and were probably much lower.

name: Operation Lucky Alphonse
sources: en.wikipedia Operation Lucky Alphonse; en.wikipedia Cyprus Emergency
borderline: A British cordon-and-search sweep with brief exchanges of fire, not a battle; en.wikipedia gives it a battle infobox ('EOKA victory')
note: Over 5,000 troops failed to catch Grivas, who escaped under fire. 7 British soldiers killed in action; 21 more died in an accidental forest fire.

name: Nicosia General Hospital (raid)
sources: Digenis Foundation EOKA calendar; Cypriot school chronologies (Μάχη στο Γενικό Νοσοκομείο Λευκωσίας)
borderline: A rescue raid with a gunfight rather than a battle
note: Raid to free Polykarpos Georkatzis, who escaped; two EOKA attackers, a British police sergeant and a Greek Cypriot pharmacist were killed.

name: Machairas
place: Afxentiou's hideout below Machairas Monastery, near Lazanias
sources: en.wikipedia Grigoris Afxentiou; el.wikipedia Γρηγόρης Αυξεντίου; eoka.org.cy; Digenis Foundation EOKA calendar
note: Betrayed by an informer, Afxentiou ordered his four companions to surrender and fought alone for some eight to ten hours, killing a British corporal; he refused to surrender ('Μολών λαβέ') and died when the British poured petrol into the dugout and set it alight.

name: Liopetri
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Liopetri; en.wikipedia Cyprus Emergency; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αχυρώνα Λιοπετρίου; eoka.org.cy
note: Also called the battle of the Liopetri barn (Achyronas): it is one battle, not two. Four-hour fight; the four refused to surrender, broke out when the barn was set on fire and were killed; one British soldier killed. Greek Cypriot sources date it 2 September, en.wikipedia 1–2 September.

name: Dikomo
place: hideout in a house at Kato Dikomo, Kyrenia district
sources: en.wikipedia Kyriakos Matsis; en.wikipedia Cyprus Emergency (Operation Filtertip); eoka.org.cy; Digenis Foundation EOKA calendar
borderline: A one-man last stand in a hideout rather than a battle; Greek Cypriot tradition calls it the battle of Dikomo
note: Matsis sent his two companions out to surrender, answered that he would come out shooting, and was killed by a grenade thrown into the hideout.

name: Omorphita
place: Omorphita (Küçük Kaymaklı), northern suburb of Nicosia
sources: en.wikipedia Bloody Christmas (1963) ('battle of Omorphita'); en.wikipedia Cypriot intercommunal violence
note: Part of Bloody Christmas. The suburb was taken and its Turkish Cypriot residents expelled; Turkish Cypriots call it a massacre, Greek Cypriots a battle.

name: Kyrenia Pass (1963)
sources: en.wikipedia Bloody Christmas (1963); en.wikipedia Bloody Christmas (1963) (pass under Turkish Cypriot control attacked from the north on 26 December by Greek Cypriots under a mainland Greek officer; Turkish Cypriots from Agirda kept it; one killed)
borderline: Described in histories of Bloody Christmas but rarely as a named battle
note: Turkish Cypriots kept control of the pass and St Hilarion; one Turkish Cypriot killed.

name: Agios Sozomenos
sources: en.wikipedia Agios Sozomenos (intercommunal violence of 6 February 1964); en.wikipedia Agios Sozomenos (violence of 6 February 1964 led to the village's abandonment)
borderline: Fighting in a mixed village; details and the battle name not verified in this pass
note: Ended with the Turkish Cypriot inhabitants abandoning the village; British troops of the Joint Truce Force intervened. Date and casualties need checking.

name: Limassol (1964)
winner_first: Greek Cypriots drew with Turkish Cypriots
sources: en.wikipedia Cypriot intercommunal violence (Limassol killings, February 1964, citing The Guardian); en.wikipedia Cypriot intercommunal violence (attacks on Turkish Cypriots persisted 'particularly in Limassol'; Guardian report of 16 February 1964)
borderline: Street fighting known as the Limassol events rather than a named battle; dates and outcome not verified in this pass
note: Greek Cypriot attack on the Turkish quarter; British mediation ended the fighting without its capture. Turkish accounts call it a massacre.

name: Ktima (Paphos)
sources: author's knowledge; not verified online in this pass; no online source found in this pass (en.wikipedia Bloody Christmas, Cypriot intercommunal violence, Battle of Tillyria and UNFICYP articles do not cover it)
borderline: Named in the checklist; dates, course and outcome not verified in this pass
note: Heavy fighting in Ktima that hastened the arrival of UNFICYP (March 1964); Turkish Cypriot fighters reportedly surrendered positions. Needs checking.

name: St Hilarion (1964)
place: St Hilarion castle and the Kyrenia pass
sources: author's knowledge; not verified online in this pass; no online source found in this pass
borderline: Greek Cypriot offensive on the TMT-held castle area; course and name not verified in this pass
note: The attack was halted under UN pressure and the Turkish Cypriots kept the castle and the pass. Needs checking.

name: Tylliria
place: Kokkina enclave and Mansoura, Tylliria, northwest Cyprus
winner_first: Greek Cypriots drew with Turkish Cypriots & Turks
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Tillyria; el.wikipedia Μάχη της Τηλλυρίας; en.wikipedia Turkish invasion of Cyprus (navbox)
note: Also called the battle of Kokkina (Turkish: Erenköy). The National Guard and the patrol boats Phaethon and Arion took Mansoura, Agios Theodoros, Alevga and Selemani and squeezed the enclave to a beachhead, but failed to take Kokkina; Turkish air strikes (8–9 August, napalm on Kato Pyrgos) hit Greek Cypriot positions and the Phaethon (7 crew killed) before a UN ceasefire. Indecisive: both sides claim success. Greek mainland officers led the National Guard.

name: Kophinou
place: Kophinou and Agios Theodoros, Larnaca district
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη της Κοφίνου; en.wikipedia Kofinou; en.wikipedia Cypriot intercommunal violence; cyprus-mail.com chronology 1967
note: The National Guard, led by Greek officers, overran the TMT positions in both villages; 24–27 Turkish Cypriots killed. A Turkish ultimatum then forced Grivas and the Greek division (some 12,000 men) out of Cyprus: a battlefield win and a strategic defeat.

name: Presidential Palace (1974 coup)
sources: en.wikipedia 1974 Cypriot coup d'état; kypros1974.moec.gov.cy (Ιστορικό); neoskosmos.com (2018)
note: National Guard tanks from Kokkinotrimithia attacked at about 08:15; the palace was burnt and Makarios escaped by the back way to Paphos. Simultaneous fighting at the police headquarters, the Tactical Reserve Unit camp and the CyBC; Nicosia was in coup hands within hours (about 100 dead in the coup overall per the Cyprus Ministry of Education; other estimates differ).

name: Archbishopric (1974 coup)
sources: en.wikipedia 1974 Cypriot coup d'état; kypros1974.moec.gov.cy (Ιστορικό); neoskosmos.com (2018)
borderline: One of the coup's Nicosia fights; little separate detail
note: Shelled by tanks and stormed; resistance there and at the police headquarters held out for some hours.

name: Limassol (1974 coup)
sources: author's knowledge; not verified online in this pass; en.wikipedia 1974 Cypriot coup d'état (no Limassol detail); neoskosmos.com 2018 (coup narrative centred on Nicosia)
borderline: Provincial resistance to the coup; details and naming not verified in this pass
note: Loyalist resistance in Limassol was crushed within a day or two. Needs checking.

name: Paphos (1974 coup)
sources: en.wikipedia 1974 Cypriot coup d'état; kypros1974.moec.gov.cy (Ιστορικό); neoskosmos.com (2018); Milliyet (19 July 1974) cited by en.wikipedia; en.wikipedia 1974 Cypriot coup d'état (Makarios fled to Paphos on 15 July and was retrieved by the British in the afternoon of 16 July; Milliyet reported violent clashes in Paphos); neoskosmos.com 2018 (junta force sent from Nicosia to Paphos)
borderline: Clashes around Makarios's refuge; details not verified in this pass
note: Makarios broadcast from Paphos ('Free Radio Paphos') and was flown out by the British on 16 July; the coup forces then took the town.

name: Kyrenia torpedo boats
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Reported military losses during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; elisme.gr (2024)
note: The two Soviet-built P-4 torpedo boats sortied from Kyrenia against the landing force; T-1 was disabled and beached (crew swam ashore), T-3 was sunk by ship and air fire with nine of ten crew killed.

name: Pente Mili (beachhead)
place: Pente Mili (Five Mile Beach), 8 km west of Kyrenia
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Pentemili beachhead; en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
note: The 251st Battalion, a T-34 platoon and artillery failed to throw back the landing; Boufas's night counterattack of 20–21 July forced a temporary Turkish withdrawal. en.wikipedia dates the battle 20–22 July and folds in the breakout to Kyrenia (separate entry here).

name: Kioneli
winner_first: Turks & Turkish Cypriots beat Greeks & Greek Cypriots
sources: en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus; en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; elisme.gr (2024)
note: ELDYK (about 550 men) with 19 tanks of the 23rd EMA attacked the enclave, which controlled the Nicosia–Kyrenia road, where Turkish paratroopers had landed; the attacks failed (tanks lost in an anti-tank ditch and to artillery).

name: Kotsakagia
place: Kotsakagia peak above the Agyrta pass, Pentadaktylos
winner_first: Greek Cypriots beat Turks & Turkish Cypriots
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Κοτζά Καγιά; en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
note: The commandos took Kotsakagia and forced a Turkish retreat from the pass, but were then ordered towards Agios Pavlos, giving up the blockade of the Nicosia–Kyrenia corridor.

name: Paphos (1974)
winner_first: Greek Cypriots & Greeks beat Turkish Cypriots
sources: en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus ('Battle of Paphos'); en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
note: The Greek LST Lesvos shelled the Turkish Cypriot positions for over two hours and landed about 450 ELDYK troops; the Turkish Cypriot militia surrendered at about 22:00.

name: Limassol (1974)
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Turkish invasion of Cyprus
borderline: The fall of a lightly armed enclave, remembered as much for atrocities as for fighting
note: Resistance collapsed about 06:00 on 22 July; about 1,000 Turkish Cypriots taken prisoner; eyewitnesses report burning, rape and killings.

name: Ledra Palace
place: Ledra Palace hotel area on the Green Line, Nicosia
winner_first: Greek Cypriots beat Turks & Turkish Cypriots
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Ledra Palace; el.wikipedia Μάχη του Λήδρα Πάλας
note: Intermittent fighting for the hotel sector through both phases; en.wikipedia scores it a Greek victory (the line held). The 336th Battalion's tank duel in the northern quarter on 15 August belongs to the same sector.

name: Kyrenia (1974)
place: Agios Georgios and the Kyrenia coast road, Kyrenia
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; kypros1974.moec.gov.cy; en.wikipedia Battle of Pentemili beachhead
note: The Turkish attack from about 11:00 broke the 33rd Commando battalion at Agios Georgios and took Kyrenia by midday, linking the beachhead with Kioneli before the ceasefire; five Turkish tanks lost. en.wikipedia treats this as the last day of the Pentemili battle.

name: Larnaca (1974)
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus (in Larnaca ceasefire talks broke down at 03:35, heavy fighting with artillery and mortars, Turkish Cypriots began surrendering by 10:30; placed after the 21 July events and before the 22 July ceasefire, with the Lefka attack at 04:45)
borderline: Attack on an enclave; thin documentation
note: Heavy fighting began when ceasefire talks failed and the enclave surrendered. The same day Lefka was attacked and Limnitis surrounded without being taken.

name: ELDYK camp (first battle)
place: ELDYK camp, between Nicosia and Gerolakkos
sources: en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus (list of ELDYK battles); en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus (list of ELDYK battles: 'The battle of the ELDYK camp (22–23 July 1974)'); en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus (no camp fighting recorded in the first phase)
borderline: Listed among ELDYK's battles on en.wikipedia; no detail found
note: The camp held until the second phase.

name: Nicosia Airport
sources: el.wikipedia Μάχη του Αεροδρομίου Λευκωσίας; en.wikipedia Operation Niki; en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
note: The Turkish assault from about 11:00 was beaten off and two M47s destroyed by bazookas; the airport then passed to UNFICYP. Operation Niki folded in: on the night of 21–22 July 13 of 15 Noratlas transports reached Nicosia from Souda; Niki-4 was shot down by Greek Cypriot anti-aircraft fire (4 crew and 27 commandos killed; 33 commandos lost in all).

name: Kyparissovouno (Hill 1024)
place: Hill 1024 (Kyparissovouno) and Kornos hill, western Pentadaktylos
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus (1–2 August 1974: 28th Division took Hill 1024 (Kiparrisavouno), B Company 31MK retook it, larger attack on 2 August took it; 316th Battalion ambush at Kornos Hill)
borderline: Fighting during the ceasefire known by the hill's height; may not be a named battle
note: The Turks took the hill on 1 August, B Company of 31 MK retook it that night, and a larger attack on 2 August took it for good; the 316th then ambushed a 28th Division column at Kornos, destroying or capturing four armoured vehicles.

name: Lapithos–Karavas
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Lapithos–Karavas; en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus (lists Lapithos and Karavas as two battles); kypros1974.moec.gov.cy
note: Turkish attack in breach of the ceasefire; the 256th, 316th and 321st battalions and an ELDYK company withdrew to the Vasilia–Vavla line after heavy losses (about 150 killed or missing).

name: Vasilia Pass
winner_first: Turks drew with Greek Cypriots & Greeks
sources: en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus ('Battle of Vasilia Passage'); en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
borderline: Mostly an artillery bombardment with no infantry assault
note: No change in positions; two Turkish M47s reported lost at Vasilia.

name: Mia Milia
place: Mia Milia and Koutsoventis, northeast of Nicosia
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Reported military losses during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
note: Opening of the second phase (Attila 2): Turkish tanks bypassed the minefields and broke through by 10:30, splitting the 399th; the 173rd anti-tank battalion was overrun and the GEEF ordered a withdrawal.

name: ELDYK camp (second battle)
place: ELDYK camp, between Nicosia and Gerolakkos
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Hellenic Force in Cyprus; el.wikipedia Σωτήρης Σταυριανάκος
note: Three attacks on 14 August were repulsed; ordered to withdraw on 15–16 August, the garrison broke out and the camp fell (ELDYK lost about 80 killed, 22 wounded, 5 missing; four or five Turkish M48s knocked out). Dates of the fall differ (15 or 16 August). ELDYK's fight at the English School on 14 August is folded in.

name: Agios Dometios
winner_first: Greeks & Greek Cypriots beat Turks & Turkish Cypriots
sources: en.wikipedia Battle of Agios Dometios
note: Scored by en.wikipedia as a Greek victory: the Turks took the neighbouring ELDYK camp but not the suburb.

name: Famagusta (1974)
place: Famagusta approaches and the walled city
winner_first: Turks & Turkish Cypriots beat Greek Cypriots
sources: en.wikipedia Military operations during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus; en.wikipedia Reported military losses during the Turkish invasion of Cyprus
note: The isolated 341st was ordered to retreat; its T-34s and 6-pounders were abandoned. Turkish units entered Famagusta and relieved the Turkish Cypriot walled city, besieged since 20 July; Varosha was left empty.
